entries.title: Obama Brushes Off White House Response to Cheesecake Factory Joke
entries.summary: “The president wasn’t even mad about the Saddam Hussein comparison,” Obama said. “But he was very upset about the Cheesecake Factory comparisons.”
entries.content:
Former President Barack Obama on Wednesday made light of the Trump administration’s response to a joke he made about The Cheesecake Factory this weekend, saying that the White House wants to deflect from economic issues by instead focusing on media squabbles.

Obama’s joke — that President Donald Trump’s White House renovations resembled former Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein opening a Cheesecake Factory — drew quick outrage this week from conservative lawmakers and President Trump, who defended The Cheesecake Factory as a "very successful company.”

But Obama mocked the president’s move to “mobilize” a response to the joke while campaigning in Georgia on Wednesday for Democrats Jon Ossoff and Keisha Lance Bottoms, arguing that the administration was more focused on vanity projects than everyday economic issues.

“The president wasn’t even mad about the Saddam Hussein comparison,” he said. “That part didn't bother him. But he was very upset about the Cheesecake Factory comparisons. He took great umbrage.”

Trump addressed the quip several times this week, including while speaking to reporters and during a campaign rally in Mississippi. The White House pushed similar messaging after Obama’s speech, hosting an hours-long YouTube livestream titled “Lo-fi Beats to Dismantle DEI To” that featured an AI-generated cartoon of Trump waving in front of a Cheesecake Factory.

The White House also staged a press conference at a Cheesecake Factory in Washington on Monday, during which Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent commented on the quality of the food and took his own shots at Obama.

“This is the man who is in charge of the economy, the person who’s supposed to be figuring out how to make your life more affordable,” Obama told the Georgia crowd, referencing Bessent’s comments. “He was out there in front of The Cheesecake Factory explaining how he ordered the delicious French cheeseburger instead of the egg rolls … These are not serious people. They don't have solutions to actual problems. So they'd rather have the media and you talking about The Cheesecake Factory."

entries.title: Judge Allows Democrats to Intervene in DOJ’s Alaska Senate Challenge
entries.summary: The Trump administration agreed to let Democrats intervene in the case after a New York Times story about the two Dan Sullivans on the ballot.
entries.content:
A federal judge in Alaska allowed Democrats to intervene in the Justice Department’s lawsuit over the state’s Senate race, setting up a decision as early as this week about whether it should be dismissed.

In an eight-page order, U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason said that Democratic candidate Mary Peltola’s campaign committee and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee can pursue their effort to have the case thrown out before the election.

“It is not readily apparent that the State will adequately represent” the interests of the campaigns and voting rights groups that requested to intervene in the lawsuit, Gleason wrote.

The DOJ had originally opposed the Democrats’ motion to intervene in its lawsuit against the state of Alaska over the race where Republican incumbent Sen. Dan S. Sullivan shares a ballot with candidate Daniel J. Sullivan.

But the Trump administration reversed its position Wednesday after The New York Times reported that the Peltola campaign and the DSCC may have been behind finding Daniel J. Sullivan, a lifelong Democrat, and recruiting him to run.

“The United States intends to seek expedited discovery from the Campaign regarding the reported conspiracy, including as to whether the Campaign attempted to deceive the Court by seeking an expedited ruling on a motion to dismiss when the Campaign may have been aware of the New York Times reporting before it was published,” the DOJ said in a court filing.

In its lawsuit, the Trump administration argued that the risk of voter confusion was too high, and that voters would confuse the incumbent senator Sullivan with the first-time candidate, who will have no party affiliation on the ballot.

The department asked the district court to pause certifying the results “pending an investigation to determine whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan.”

“The sole purpose of his candidacy is to benefit the Peltola campaign by reducing the number of votes for Senator Sullivan,” the DOJ said in its lawsuit.

Polling from the Times puts Peltola ahead, while the Cook Political Report has the race as a toss up.

Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska), who in days prior was showing support for the Peltola campaign in the lawsuit, changed her tune on Wednesday.

“Alaskans deserve the honest truth from Mary and her campaign—what has been revealed is a pattern of lies and coverups and a culture of deception that belongs nowhere in our elections or among our elected officials,” Murkowski said in a statement.

In a court filing Wednesday, the campaign and DSCC did not address the Times story. Instead, the defendants continued to argue that the case “is about whether DOJ can enjoin Alaska’s lawful certification of the U.S. Senate election if the President’s preferred candidate loses.”

President Donald Trump has made his distaste of the matter clear since the lawsuit.

“The Democrats’ false statements were made under oath in Federal Court. Therefore, they perjured themselves, and should be liable for very serious consequences,” Trump said in a Truth Social post on Wednesday. “Mary Peltola should suffer the Legal and Political consequences for what she has done, A FRAUD ON THE AMERICAN PUBLIC, and Dan Sullivan should be allowed to run without either Mary Peltola or FAKE Dan Sullivan on the Ballot.”

Blanche defended the lawsuit on CNN’s Sunday show. When asked what crime the state committed in allowing both Sullivans on the ballot, Blanche responded, “There could be a crime.”

Following the Times report, Blanche doubled down.

“Let's call it what it is: They are cheating. They are trying to take votes away from the incumbent, not by running an election and not by running on issues, but by putting up a person with the same name so they confuse Alaskans,” he said on Fox News.

entries.title: Federal Judge Rules DOJ Cannot Segregate California Ballots
entries.summary: The ruling lands after several days in court, where the Justice Department’s arguments did not seem to land or hold up to scrutiny.
entries.content:
A federal judge on Wednesday declined a Justice Department request to stop California from counting the votes of over 20,000 people the government identified as potential noncitizen voters.

U.S. District Judge David O. Carter ruled that the government’s request to segregate a tranche of ballots was delivered too late in the elections process and that their attempts to isolate noncitizen voters lacked credibility, potentially leading to erroneously disenfranchised voters.

“This Court will not deprive Californians who have met the requirements for voter registration of their fundamental right because of Plaintiff’s unfounded allegations,” Carter wrote.

The Justice Department late Wednesday appealed the ruling to the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals.

California and the Justice Department have been in a legal back-and-forth over alleged noncitizens on the state’s voter rolls since July, when the Department of Homeland Security said it had identified 190,832 potential noncitizen voters on California’s rolls.

By October, that number was lowered to 20,000 names, which were sent in a list to the Los Angeles County clerk on a password-protected thumb drive. California election officials were instructed to hold on to the ballots of people listed or set aside completed ballots submitted by people on the thumb drive until their citizenship could be verified.

At a hearing Tuesday, the DOJ asked the court to force California to set aside the ballots of any person identified on the list it shared with county officials in October, while the state wanted the judge to effectively stop the Justice Department from interfering with the state’s election administration.

In the 26-page order, Carter criticized the government for what he said was an attempt to coerce a state government into abandoning its procedures on the eve of an election.

He said that allowing the Trump administration to sequester ballots using “faulty data sources that sweep in U.S. citizens” would permit the president and his allies to create “chaos for their own political purposes” to disrupt the election.

“Over 20,000 registered Californians would potentially lose the right that generations of Americans have fought to preserve,” Carter wrote. “In bringing this lawsuit, the Executive would have this Court believe that it reigns as a sole sovereign. But California and its people are sovereign, too.”

Carter added that the existing federal criminal code is sufficient to allow federal law enforcement to prosecute noncitizens for voting in U.S. elections, and said California has procedures of its own to cancel ineligible voter registrations.

“The Executive’s requested relief, however, would wreak havoc and disrupt the election that is already underway, create a chilling effect on election workers and voters alike, and discount the votes of United States citizens,” Carter said. “The Executive Branch cannot replace the remedy Congress carefully enacted with its own unlawful and unconstitutional solution instead.”

The Justice Department had charged 28 people with noncitizen registration or voting in California, and it has continued to make publicized arrests as a part of “Operation Protect the Vote.”

Carter told the DOJ, in reference to the arrests made in California of alleged noncitizens in October, that it can continue to charge noncitizens but cannot tell California how to count or not count certain ballots.

Attorneys for California said they had heard the Justice Department had threatened election officials with criminal prosecution if they tabulated the ballots of those on this list.

After a short recess, Carter said at the hearing’s conclusion, “This court believes it would be wise that any threats to state and county elected employees cease immediately.”

Attorneys for the state also said there are no state laws or regulations in California that allow ballots to be segregated without informing a voter. County officials would have to review ballots by hand and not process them.

This story has been updated with further information from the court ruling and the appeal filed by the Justice Department.

entries.title: Capitals Beat Flyers, 5-2
entries.summary: Alex Tuch became only the second player in Capitals history to score at least nine goals in his first 11 games for the team.
entries.content:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Alex Tuch scored his eighth and ninth goals in his first season with Washington, the second into an empty net to help the Capitals seal a 5-2 victory over the Philadelphia Flyers on Wednesday night.

Tuch arrived in a trade from Buffalo and signed an eight-year, $84-million contract extension in June. On Wednesday, he became only the second player in Capitals history to score at least nine goals in his first 11 games for the team, joining Dino Ciccarelli, who scored 12 times in his first 11 Caps appearances to close the 1988-89 season.

Jordan Kyrou also scored twice, and Aliaksei Protas added his first goal of the season as Washington completed a five-game homestand with four wins.

Dylan Strome had three assists, and Jack St. Ivany and Pierre-Luc Dubois each had two. Logan Thompson made 23 saves after missing a victory Saturday against Buffalo because of a lower-body injury.

Matvei Michkov scored his ninth goal of the season and fifth on the power play for Philadelphia, which lost its third straight after an overtime defeat to visiting Columbus on Tuesday night.

Sean Couturier leveled it early in the second, and Joseph Woll made 25 stops for the Flyers.

Tuch got started only 1:50 into the game.

St. Ivany put the initial attempt on Woll’s net from outside the right faceoff circle, and Strome got a stick to the rebound before Tuch one-timed the puck past Woll from the slot.

Tuch put the game away more than 55 minutes later, taking a feed from Dubois on the break to score easily against the Flyers' 6-on-5.

entries.title: D.C. United Falls to Toronto FC, 2-1
entries.summary: The team was eliminated from playoff contention.
entries.content:
TORONTO (AP) — Josh Sargent scored a go-ahead goal in the 86th minute to help Toronto FC beat D.C. United 2-1 on Wednesday night.

Sargent calmly slotted home a rebound for his ninth goal of the season after Theo Corbeanu’s shot bounced off the post. It was the ninth time this season Toronto has scored a tying or go-ahead goal in the final 10 minutes of a game.

Toronto (9-11-12), which finished its home schedule with a 6-2-9 record, needed the win after entering three points outside of a wild-card spot in the Eastern Conference.

D.C. United (7-13-12) was eliminated from playoff contention.

Andre Dozzell scored his first goal for D.C. United in the 29th minute. Dozzell settled a back pass from Silvan Hefti and sent a low shot off the right hand of a diving Luka Gavran that went inside the far post.

Toronto tied it at 1-all in the 63rd on its first shot on target. Sargent elevated for a header that deflected off Jonathan Osorio's back and past goalkeeper Sean Johnson. The goal, originally given to Sargent, was initially disallowed due to an offside flag but a video review confirmed it was a good goal.

entries.title: Alaska’s Governor Has Ordered an Investigation Into the Senate Race
entries.summary: “Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections,” Gov. Mike Dunleavy posted on X.
entries.content:
Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy ordered an investigation into Democrats’ reported plan to stack the state’s Senate ballot with a second candidate named Dan Sullivan.

The Republican governor accused Democrats of trying to “deliberately confuse voters and misdirect their votes.”

“The evidence will determine what happens next,” Dunleavy posted on X.

The governor did not specify what laws may have been broken.

“Alaskans have a fundamental right to vote for the candidate they actually intend to support,” he wrote. “Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections.”

Dunleavy’s order comes after a frantic 24 hours in Alaskan politics. The New York Times reported that Democratic candidate Mary Peltola’s campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee secretly recruited candidates into the race, ultimately Dan J. Sullivan, who shares a name with the incumbent Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan.

The DSCC and the Peltola campaign have both denied being involved in the ballot-stacking plan.

Following the Times’ reporting, President Donald Trump said Peltola should face “legal and political consequences.” Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) called the plan “a pattern of lies and coverups.”

Ballot-stacking strategies have been employed by both parties for years and some Democrats have, if not outright defended the alleged actions of the Peltola campaign, pointed to examples of Republicans engaging in similar behavior.

In 2024, when Peltola was running for reelection to the House, the state Republican Party legally backed a Democrat on the ballot who had just begun a 20 year prison sentence across the country. The candidate is on the ballot again this year.

Last Friday, the Trump administration preemptively sued the state of Alaska, effectively laying out its plan for contesting a race outcome where the incumbent Republican loses, citing potential voter confusion. On Wednesday night, a federal judge allowed Democrats to intervene in the case, teeing up a decision as soon as this week.

entries.title: The Washington Sun Metro: JLG’s Pay Check
entries.content:
Good morning. This is The Washington Sun Metro Newsletter for Oct. 29, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

In today’s newsletter: Mayoral pay, the delegate dilemma and AJ Dybantsa’s debut. 

Capital Weather’s Daily Digit — 9/10: A few morning clouds are no bother. Brilliant sunshine takes over, with mild temperatures making for another fall stunner. Read the full forecast.

THE LATEST

The politics of pay are at play in D.C.

Likely mayor-to-be Janeese Lewis George tells The Washington Sun’s Martin Austermuhle that she opposes a bill working its way through the D.C. Council that would increase the mayoral salary from $250,000 to $290,000.

“Families in this city are stretched on child care, housing and their utility bills, and I am not going to ask them to pay more for the job of the mayor,” she said.

D.C. law doesn’t allow any adjustments to the mayor’s pay during their term, so lawmakers often make any changes in the two months between an election and inauguration. The last pay bump was approved in late 2022.

But the political context now is very different. D.C. is facing leaner budgets, Lewis George campaigned on improving affordability and unions representing some 10,000 government workers are agitating for more money after outgoing Mayor Muriel Bowser’s negotiators offered them no cost-of-living adjustments for the next few years.

“Public service deserves fair compensation at every level of government, but fairness cannot be reserved for those at the top,” said Joey Davis, president of AFGE Local 1975, which represents 1,200 workers in agencies from the Department of Public Works to the Department of Motor Vehicles.

Earlier this year, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani turned down an 18% pay raise that lawmakers had approved.





DEEP DIVE


Robert White Jr. (6000x4000, AR: 1.50)
At-Large D.C. Council member Robert White has set a Monday deadline to either secure a legal fix or resign his seat to preserve his run for congressional delegate, The Sun’s Michael Brice-Saddler reports.

Facing a 1970 D.C. law that bars the delegate from holding another paid public office on the “date of his election,” White announced Wednesday that he will step down by Monday if an emergency legislative or legal solution falls through.

White is publicly pushing back against the D.C. attorney general’s interpretation that he must resign before Tuesday. In a statement, White argued the law’s language refers to the date election results are certified in December, not the date voters go to the polls. Having to resign early, White said, would be “fundamentally undemocratic” and would interrupt his legislative work while forcing taxpayers to foot the bill for two separate special elections.

The maneuvering has already sparked some political friction. The D.C. Democratic Party issued a preemptive warning Wednesday, asserting its authority under the Home Rule Charter to appoint an interim council member. The party signaled it is already working to fill the anticipated vacancy and issued a sharp rebuke against any legislative workarounds, calling any attempt to circumvent its appointment process “an attack on Home Rule itself.”

A legislative fix seems highly unlikely, regardless. Speaking to reporters Wednesday, White said that Council Chair Phil Mendelson indicated he would not be advancing an emergency bill to resolve the issue. With that path obstructed, White says he will spend the next few days weighing an emergency court filing or stepping down.





FROM THE DISTRICT

Concepts of a closed course: The Trump administration confirmed to a federal judge that the government is “working to develop a plan” to close East Potomac Golf Links for redevelopment by Nov. 15, The Sun’s Justice Covert reports.

The Trump administration is doubling down on plans to use the president’s proposed triumphal arch as a military complex, The Sun’s Kendall Staton reports. In court filings Wednesday, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth argued that the 250-foot monument could help protect the nation from coordinated drone attacks.

Controversy on 17th Street: A drag queen dressed as Tina Turner stole the show and (nearly) the win at Tuesday’s 39th annual 17th Street High Heel Race, WTOP reports, rushing from the crowd to cut in front of the competitors at the end of the race to initially claim first prize.





FROM MARYLAND

A Prince George’s County elementary school is closing for the rest of the week after at least 48 students and 16 staff members reported “influenza-like and gastroenteritis-like symptoms,” WTOP reports. Princeton Elementary will be deep cleaned and sanitized, with a particular focus on the cafeteria, classrooms, bathrooms and high-touch surfaces.





TALK TO TOM


Tom Sietsema is back answering your questions about the D.C. dining scene. Submit your questions here. 

You’re celebrating your 10th anniversary. Where do you go?

I’d spring for a restaurant with some nice age on it. The well-regarded Centrolina and The Dabney represent the class of 2015 and offer Italian and Mid-Atlantic flavors, respectively. But they’re babies compared to some of the area’s longer-lived establishments: Obelisk in Dupont Circle, Perry’s in Adams Morgan, the Bombay Club near the White House, Il Pizzico in Rockville, La Ferme in Chevy Chase, L’Auberge Chez Francois in Great Falls and the fabled, nearly-50 Inn at Little Washington in Washington, Virginia.

The most senior of the bunch, though, is Old Ebbitt Grill, whose revolving door never seems to stop and whose hospitality remains something to emulate even at … 170 years.

In the full Q&A: How to get a reservation at Albi, international food consultants and Dublin recs. 





SPORTS

Matt LeCroy AP - 26122031238347 (4000x2667, AR: 1.50)
On the first day of Nationals spring training, Matthew LeCroy introduces himself to players with a joke: “AAA manager. I’m the guy none of you want to meet.” They laugh for two reasons: because it’s funny and because it’s true. LeCroy, to be clear, is a pleasant guy. But AAA, according to him, is maybe the hardest level in affiliated baseball, The Washington Sun’s Jesse Dougherty writes. And for the past six years, LeCroy has managed there in the Nationals’ organization.

One of the best parts of his role is delivering the news that players are headed to the majors. But that also means the job comes with a blunt reality: When LeCroy is doing it well, he’s sending player after player to the place he also wants to go, as he keeps dreaming of managing in the big leagues.

AJ Dybantsa has arrived. After sitting out the first four games of the season with an ankle injury, the No. 1 overall pick made his official Wizards debut on Wednesday night against the Cavaliers. The rookie forward started hot, scoring 9 points in his first seven minutes. He finished with 19 on the night, giving Wizards fans something to savor in a 121-111 defeat.

entries.title: Morning Sun: The Alaska Gambit
entries.content:
Today’s notice: The latest from an increasingly dramatic election map. A scoop about White House efforts to find buyers for Russian diesel. Democrats’ 2028 agenda includes figuring out how to campaign in the age of AI. And: A story about Northampton, Massachusetts, and the cruel politics of deep-blue America. 

THE MAP

Alaska: Wild country, wild times. “This is a scandal of the highest order,” Dan Sullivan (the senator, that is) told Fox News last night. His advice to voters: “Don’t let Democrats cheat.”

Where we are: On the one hand, there is the Justice Department effort to toss out the Senate election results if the Republican incumbent does not win. That effort has been roundly condemned by a broad swath of people, including Republican Sen. Lisa Murkowski. A federal judge last night allowed Democrats to intervene in the DOJ lawsuit, and the same judge could dismiss the whole case by Friday.

On the other hand, there is the revelation that what Donald Trump and his allies have alleged about the Alaska Senate race appears to be true: Democrats did set out to confuse voters by recruiting the other Dan Sullivan to run, according to a seemingly airtight New York Times report yesterday. People who think the lawsuit is bupkis do not think the Times story is. Murkowski accused Democrat Mary Peltola’s campaign of a “cover-up,” while Trump posted that Peltola should face “legal and political consequences.”

He may get one of those, but not the other. The lawsuit remains on very shaky legal ground, and running for office to make it harder for another candidate to win is not illegal. But there’s still time for voters to punish Peltola for the trickery. Or, at least, for Republicans playing defense to make that their closing argument.

Meanwhile, in the Lower 48:

Ohio: That ad, and dat ass. That’s what the marquee races in this state have come down to, The Washington Sun’s Al Weaver reports from Lima. Republican gubernatorial nominee Vivek Ramaswamy’s ad featuring Democrat Amy Acton’s estranged mother has blotted out practically everything else, Al writes. Whatever is left has been drowned out by the president’s ongoing fascination with Sen. Jon Husted’s butt. “None of that was on my bingo card,” Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose, a Republican, told The Sun.

Georgia: Barack Obama is back at The Cheesecake Factory. Trump “wasn’t even mad about the Saddam Hussein comparison,” the former president told a crowd in Atlanta. “That part didn’t bother him. But he was very upset about the Cheesecake Factory comparisons. He took great umbrage.”

To the haters, Obama said he knows how to navigate a chain-restaurant menu. “I am the father of two daughters,” he said. “Do you think I could have survived their childhood without going to The Cheesecake Factory? … That was my jam for about a decade.”

Iowa: The cancer crisis election. The state ranks second in the nation for new cancer diagnoses, and talk about how to deal with the increasing numbers has played a dominant role this election cycle, The Sun’s Elena Schneider reports from Maxwell. More than $20 million has been spent by both parties airing ads referring to cancer. In 2022, that figure was less than $200,000. “Everyone knows someone with cancer,” a national GOP strategist told Elena. “These voters are saying, ‘Holy crap, this is a big problem, and Republicans have been in charge for over a decade,’ so there’s no other place to point finger.”

Florida: Democrats change their mind. House Democrats’ super PAC rebought ad time in two congressional districts — Florida’s 7th and 27th — where it had recently canceled its buys. The previous withdrawal spurred speculation that House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries was abandoning the races, though the new ad reservations are for less than was planned before.

Michigan: Fiancé-gate and the neverending primary. Rep. Haley Stevens’ fiancé said he’s voting for Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers over Stevens’ opponent in the Democratic primary, Abdul El-Sayed. There’s little love lost between the camps: CNN reported El-Sayed and Stevens haven’t spoken in months, though she did say on the network last night that she’s voting for El-Sayed. Republicans are banking on the ongoing strife among Democrats to put Rogers over the top.

California: DOJ told to leave the ballots alone. U.S. District Judge David O. Carter declined a DOJ request yesterday to stop California from counting the votes of over 20,000 people the government identified as potential noncitizen voters. “This Court will not deprive Californians who have met the requirements for voter registration of their fundamental right because of Plaintiff’s unfounded allegations,” Carter ruled. The DOJ instantly appealed to the 9th Circuit.

Maine: Troy Jackson wins mock election. The annual statewide student “election” run through the secretary of state’s office “has shown an exceptional capacity for predicting the state’s real election outcomes,” the Portland Press Herald reports, except for the 2020 matchup between Republican Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Sara Gideon. So Democrats should be either really excited by Jackson’s mock win this week — or really worried.

Mississippi: Dems investing to boost Scott Colom. The DSCC bought $500,000 in ad time for the nominee yesterday, the first time the campaign arm has made that kind of investment in the state this cycle.

More: Democrats Seek to Close the ‘Elon Musk Loophole’ in Campaign Spending • Crypto Went Big for Republicans After Democrats Sank the CLARITY Act • Civil Rights Groups Sue to Stop DHS Voter Fraud Investigations

FROM THE WHITE HOUSE

Scoop: Trump aides trying to find buyers for Russian oil. At least three vessels carrying Russian fuel released through Trump’s deal with Vladimir Putin are expected to make it across the Atlantic the week after the midterms. The question is, who will accept it? The Sun’s Anna Kramer and Jeff Stein report that administration officials are privately encouraging U.S. firms to accept the oil, but the firms are hesitant due to the legal and political liabilities of accepting sanctioned fuel.

FROM 2028


First on The Sun: Top Democrats to discuss how to deal with AI campaigning after 2026. How Weird Will AI Make 2028? will be among the topics of conversation when Democrats gather for the centrist What’s Next conference in Denver shortly after ballots are counted next week. The Sun’s Jenna Monnin got a first look at the programming for the event, as well as an expanded list of Democrats attending, including Sen. Michael Bennet of Colorado, Reps. Jamie Raskin of Maryland and Chris Deluzio of Pennsylvania and a slew of mayors from across the country.

NEW ON THE WASHINGTON SUN

Deep-blue America is not OK: First came the story of that western Massachusetts lesbian bar. Now comes the tale of a downtown redevelopment plan in Northampton, where the language and tactics of national political warfare have filtered into this small town. The Sun’s Ellie Silverman takes a deep dive into the breakdown of civic life there — a world where everyone is a Democrat, everyone is woke, everyone knows everyone and everyone calls everyone else a fascist.

entries.title: Iowa’s Cancer Crisis Has Upended Pivotal Midterm Races
entries.summary: In the state’s tight races for Senate and governor, both parties are focusing on an issue that has rocketed to the front of voters’ minds.
entries.content:
MAXWELL, Iowa — Eight days from Election Day, Rob Sand is surrounded by knee-high grasses, surveying a wetlands nature preserve. This brief hike, in the waning hours of his hotly contested gubernatorial campaign, is tied to the issue roiling races up and down the ballot here: the cancer crisis.

Expanding the state’s wetlands is one part of the Democratic candidate’s plan to address the skyrocketing rates of cancer in Iowa, which ranks second-highest for new cancer diagnoses. Wetlands can improve water quality, which has been identified as one of several factors contributing to Iowa’s crisis. Sand’s Republican opponent, Zach Lahn, also lists wetlands expansion in his own cancer plan.

“I’m glad that we have two candidates that are willing to talk about funding” environmental projects focused on improving water quality, Sand told reporters Monday. “It’s a huge issue in this race that a lot of people find incredibly motivating.”

But who voters ultimately blame for this crisis will be a core factor for whether Democrats are able to flip the state that backed President Donald Trump by successively larger percentages starting in 2016. Iowa Democrats believe there’s an opening for Sand and state Rep. Josh Turek, who is running for Senate, in this red state.

Democrats say it’s more than just cancer that could give them an edge here, pointing to deepening frustration over the Iran war, high gas prices and a chaotic tariff trade regime. As evidence of the stiff headwinds, the Congressional Leadership Fund — the flagship GOP super PAC — cut off its spending on behalf of Iowa Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks by mid-October.

Republicans privately acknowledge that opening for statewide races, too.

Sign up for The Stakeout, The Sun's Congress newsletter you actually want to read. 

“Everyone knows someone with cancer,” a national Republican consultant said of the situation in Iowa. They, like others who spoke to The Washington Sun, were granted anonymity to discuss the issue candidly. “These voters are saying, ‘Holy crap, this is a big problem, and Republicans have been in charge for over a decade,’ so there’s no other place to point finger.”

One Iowa Republican strategist called cancer “a liability for Republicans” and said it’s “a liability because of their past actions in the legislature.” It’s dragging down the entire ticket, the strategist acknowledged, while the party also is “suffering from an enthusiasm gap this whole cycle.”

But the cancer crisis — and who to blame, and what to do about it — moved to the fore of debates, TV ads and campaign events this cycle in Iowa, a once-unthinkable reality given the state’s dependence on its agriculture industry. Cancer and water quality regularly rank among the top three issues for voters across the state, according to private polling of state legislative races shared with The Washington Sun.

More than $20 million has been spent by both parties airing ads referring to cancer specifically, according to AdImpact, the ad-tracking firm. In 2022, less than $200,000 was spent on ads that mentioned cancer.

Lahn, a businessman and farmer, put cancer at the center of his insurgent Republican primary campaign for governor this spring, becoming the face of the state’s “Make America Healthy Again” movement. As a first-time candidate, he beat the Trump-endorsed Republican, Rep. Randy Feenstra, in the primary. He did it all while blaming Big Ag and chemical companies for their role in the state’s rising cancer rates.

That’s put him at odds with some of the traditional, GOP-aligned forces in the state.

“They all talk about it as a problem, but no one’s talking about the real issue, which is farming, so Lahn is an anomaly when it comes to a Republican actually really talking about it,” said state Rep. Jennifer Konfrst, a Democrat. “It’s hanging right there, but no one’s going to grab it because no one wants to piss off the farmers.”

The gubernatorial candidates are trading shots over their connections to the cancer crisis in TV ads blanketing the state’s airwaves. Lahn accuses Sand’s “biggest donor” of getting “caught polluting your drinking water” while “Iowa cancer rates” are rising. And Sand, in his own ads, attacks Lahn for supporting “budget cuts that slashed cancer research funding” and backing “a plan that would bankrupt rural hospitals.” But pro-Sand groups are outspending pro-Lahn efforts in TV ads, $38 million to $32 million, according to AdImpact.

Iowa state Sen. Molly Donahue, a Democrat who attended Sand’s canvass launch in Cedar Rapids last weekend, said voters are “absolutely” connecting the cancer crisis to who they vote for. But she isolated those who might flip to voting for a Democrat as the “moderate Republicans who absolutely agree” on who to blame. “We’re never going to convince the MAGA crowd,” she added.

“I mean, there are a few who have flipped,” she said, “a few, but not many.”
Rob Sand in Iowa (5712x4284, AR: 1.33)In a statement, a Lahn campaign spokesman said that “career politicians like Rob Sand have had plenty of chances to tackle the cancer crisis,” but “they’ve failed because they don’t do hard things. Zach is an outsider who has never run for office before. He’ll stand up to the special interests with fresh, new ideas that will make Iowa the best place to live.”

Sand, the state’s auditor, is the lone elected Democrat to survive the state’s red-leaning realignment over the past decade. He’s raised more than double the cash Lahn has brought in, and national Democrats believe he’s one of the best-positioned candidates to flip a governor’s mansion. He has campaigned on “a crisis of costs, corruption and cancer,” while trying to shake free of the national Democratic Party label.

He’s also zeroed in on Lahn’s residency in Iowa: Public voting records show that Lahn voted in Kansas in 2018, 2020 and 2022, before registering to vote in Iowa in 2024.

“At the end of the day, people can trust me because they've seen my actions across the state of Iowa over time, and know that what I'm saying is stuff that I've actually — they can trust my actions that speak louder than words,” Sand said Monday.

Like Sand, Turek is also leaning into the cancer crisis in the final stretch of the campaign. In an interview with The Sun, he recounted how his sister, who lives in Council Bluffs, was diagnosed with Stage 2 breast cancer “nearly the day” he launched his Senate campaign. She hasn’t been able to get her insurance to cover a PET scan, Turek said, to see if her cancer spread because it was Stage 2, not 3 or 4, and they “basically said, ‘Sorry, you don't have enough cancer.’”

“I think more and more people are paying attention to who actually cares about the health care crisis and the cancer crisis and the water quality crisis, and who is legitimately going to address it,” he said.

Turek’s sister now appears in an ad running in the closing days of the campaign.

His opponent in the Senate race, Rep. Ashley Hinson, considered a star recruit by Republicans, has also advocated for more funding into cancer research. In a statement, National Republican Senatorial Committee spokeswoman Samantha Cantrell said that Hinson “wants to get Iowa’s cancer rates down quickly,” citing her recent bipartisan legislation to expand access to cancer screenings.

“Ashley will work with anyone to lower healthcare costs and get Iowa’s cancer rates under control,” Cantrell added.

Scott Kaas, a self-described “conservative Republican” who has “never voted for a Democrat in my life,” appeared in a digital ad on behalf of Turek, an endorsement based on their work to pass a bill funding pediatric cancer research. Kaas’ now 4-year-old daughter, Devyn, was diagnosed with bone marrow cancer at 7 months old and he started advocating on behalf of pediatric cancer patients soon after. She’s now in remission, he said.

But Kaas isn’t sure whether Turek’s work on cancer funding will persuade voters to do what he’s doing and cross party lines.

“Not many that I’ve spoken to,” Kaas said. “Honestly, they’re either a Republican or a Democrat, and that’s just the way they’re going to vote.”

entries.title: A Pay Bump for D.C.’s Next Mayor? Janeese Lewis George Says No.
entries.summary: The likely next mayor opposes a bill that would raise the position’s salary from $250,000 to $290,000.
entries.content:
D.C.’s likely mayor-to-be is turning down what could be a $40,000 pay raise.

Ward 4 council member Janeese Lewis George — the Democratic nominee in next Tuesday’s mayoral election — tells The Washington Sun that she opposes a bill moving through the D.C. Council that would bump the mayoral salary next year to $290,000, up from the $250,000 that the current mayor, Muriel Bowser, has been making since 2023.

"Families in this city are stretched on child care, housing and their utility bills, and I am not going to ask them to pay more for the job of the mayor,” she said. “My focus is on lowering costs for the hardworking people of D.C.”

The bill was quietly introduced this month by At-Large council member Anita Bonds, who said on Wednesday that the raise would “better reflect modern cost realities.”

Lewis George says she did not request the measure, and Bowser’s office confirmed it also didn’t come from them. But it mirrors the last bill authorizing a pay raise for the mayor that the council passed in late 2022.

The pay for D.C.’s chief executive cannot be increased during their four-year term, so any push to do so has to happen in the two months between when an election takes place and the mayor assumes office. Adjusting the mayor’s pay also impacts the council chair and attorney general, both of whom, by law, have to make $10,000 less than the mayor.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Council Chair Phil Mendelson declined to specify whether he supports or spurred the introduction of the current bill. Attorney General Brian Schwalb’s office did not comment.

Bowser’s pay puts her among the 10 most well-remunerated mayors in the U.S., with the chief executives of cities like New York, Los Angeles and San Francisco standing ahead of her. Still, the role of D.C. mayor is distinct to those of many other big-city leaders. D.C. has no official mayoral residence, for one, and the city also operates as a county and state.

D.C.’s mayor also isn’t the highest-paid employee in the government. Interim Police Chief Jeffery Carroll, for example, makes $319,000 a year, while Maurice Edington, the president of the University of the District of Columbia, makes $310,000.

That Lewis George turned down the pay raise likely reflects her mayoral campaign’s focus on affordability for D.C. residents, as well as an understanding of the problematic optics of taking home a bigger salary as the city faces leaner budgets to come — including a deficit next year that could reach $800 million. Earlier this year, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani declined an 18% salary bump that was approved by city lawmakers, saying that voters had never told him “their concern is that the mayor makes too little.”

The median household income in D.C. in 2025 was $107,600. Council members currently make $171,000 a year.

The debate over the D.C. mayor’s salary also comes at a politically fraught time. On Wednesday — the same day that Bonds’ committee held a hearing on her bill — hundreds of unionized city employees rallied outside the Wilson Building to protest what they say is a proposed contract for some 10,000 workers that would see no cost-of-living adjustments at all for the coming years — on top of not having received one over the last year.

Bonds’ bill would also provide new, annual cost-of-living increases.

“Public service deserves fair compensation at every level of government, but fairness cannot be reserved for those at the top,” said Joey Davis, the president of AFGE Local 1975, which represents some 1,200 workers in agencies ranging from the Department of Public Works to the Department of Motor Vehicles.

“The mayor does not collect the trash, the mayor does not fix the roads or perform the countless daily functions that allow the city to function,” he added. “City employees do … and the city employees who make that possible deserve compensation that reflects their contributions.”

Managing these demands from D.C.’s unionized workers will be one of many challenges facing Lewis George, who was widely supported by organized labor ahead of the competitive June primary. While D.C. has recently finalized new contracts and pay raises for teachers and police officers, there’s little money left in the city’s Workforce Investments Account — which is used to pay out the cost of new contracts — over the next year. As of this week the account has $130 million in it, with $122 million already set aside for a new contract for D.C. firefighters.

“We are not extra. We are not optional. We are essential,” said Robert Alston, the president of AFSCME Local 2921, which represents educational aides in D.C. Public Schools. “It isn’t only about a paycheck, but it’s about our dignity, our respect and fairness. This is about recognizing the value of the people who show up every day.”

entries.title: In Ohio, an Ad and an Ass Take Center Stage
entries.summary: “None of that was on my bingo card,” Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose told The Sun.
entries.content:
LIMA, Ohio — An ad and an ass are consuming Ohio’s political scene.

Just days before Election Day, a pair of topics have come out of left field in the final sprint and are overshadowing the Iran war and the economy, both of which dominated the campaign up until now.

The headliner is Republican Vivek Ramaswamy’s decision to broadcast an ad featuring Donna Arthur, the mother of Amy Acton — his Democratic opponent in the gubernatorial contest — accusing her of being a liar and having mental health issues. Acton's mother lost custody of Acton and her brother after her husband was indicted on suspicion of sexually abusing Acton, who was 12 years old at the time. She hasn’t spoken to her mother in nearly 50 years.

The other is Sen. Jon Husted’s rear end, which President Donald Trump has admired and spoken about at length at multiple rallies. It’s become a running joke on the campaign trail as the Republican incumbent looks to defeat former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown.

“None of that was on my bingo card,” Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose told The Washington Sun in a brief interview about the issues now at the forefront in the final days of campaigning.

Once a preeminent swing state that has turned reliably red over the past decade, Ohio Democrats are salivating at the prospect of winning a spate of races, having not won a statewide contest since 2008 that did not feature Brown.

They likely have their best chance in the governor’s race, where Acton, the former director of the state’s Department of Health during the COVID-19 pandemic, has a good shot at nabbing it for Democrats for the first time since 2006.

Sign up for The Stakeout, The Sun's Congress newsletter you actually want to read. 

Acton had opened up a lead in public polls over the last month, but saw the race explode when the ad featuring her estranged mother appeared in Ohio. The ad also caught attention nationally, and it eventually emerged that Ramaswamy’s campaign was behind it and paid $4 million to put it on the airwaves,

While Trump and Vice President JD Vance have both backed the controversial spot, the overall blowback has been fierce — and bipartisan. Husted quickly distanced himself from the ad, telling reporters on Wednesday that he “wouldn’t have run” it. Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine, a Republican, called for Ramaswamy to take down the ad, and other Republicans indicated that they viewed it as a mistake.

“The question is: Should you run it?” said Rep. Bob Latta (R-Ohio). “If it were me, I probably wouldn’t have.”

Ohio Politics 2026 (8396x5598, AR: 1.50)At an event on Monday in Dayton that featured Acton, Brown and musician John Legend, speaker after speaker whacked the ad. Legend, a native of nearby Springfield, labeled Ramaswamy “desperate” and “despicable” for the move.

Outside those in the White House, few Republicans are lining up to defend Ramaswamy, especially amid fears that the attack ad was a failed Hail Mary attempt.

A pair of Republican operatives with knowledge of internal polling said that Ramaswamy’s support has cratered since the ad went public, with his numbers shifting from a margin-of-error race versus Acton to facing a mid- to high-single-digit deficit.

Husted’s support, however, remains relatively unchanged, according to these operatives. The surveys show him still in a margin-of-error contest with Brown, though there’s some fear that Ramaswamy could ultimately drag him down..

“Vivek was losing and is going to lose, and that certainly did not help him. I think Husted is getting closer and closing, and Republicans were coming home,” said one Republican operative with Ohio ties, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to candidly discuss the state of play. “[Ramaswamy] is incredibly unlikable.”

A new Suffolk University poll also showed that 72% of respondents had seen or heard the ad, with Ramaswamy’s unfavorable rating ticking up by 2 points since its previous survey in September.

Overall, Acton leads in the survey by 4 percentage points, with limited movement among voters on either side after the ad.

The Ramaswamy campaign did not respond to a request for comment on their internal polling.

Adding to his troubles, The Cook Political Report also shifted the race to “lean Democrat.”

“It’s not going over well,” John Kulewicz, the Democratic nominee to become Ohio’s attorney general, told The Sun. “It reflects what [Ramaswamy] thinks of the people of Ohio, and it’s not very flattering.”

As for Husted, his rear end has inexplicably become one of the biggest talking points in his race to win his first full Senate term and thwart the return of Brown, a former three-term member. Gov. Mike DeWine appointed Husted in January 2025 to finish Vance’s term, when he shifted to his role as vice president.

20261028_mcgarvey_OHGOP_1221.jpg (7863x5242, AR: 1.50)20261028_mcgarvey_OHGOP_4846.jpg (8187x5461, AR: 1.50)During a pair of events in Northwest Ohio, speaker after speaker couldn't help but get in jokes about Husted’s posterior.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune said that his Senate colleague has “got it going on.” (He also told The Sun that he works out with Husted daily in the Senate gym and “that guy can get after it.” He declined to comment further on his “physique.”)

CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz chimed in: “I've never gotten the compliments he's received from the president, even though I've known the president for 20-something years. But I'm not jealous.”

Sen. Bernie Moreno chose to use a pun, saying, “The only ass we should be talking about is Sherrod Brown.”

Moreno also noted his fellow Ohio senator’s rear end has become the topic du jour in his preelection travels — even outside of his home state.

“I was meeting with the president on Saturday [in Washington] and literally my Uber driver asked me where I’m from. I said Ohio, and he said, ‘Oh, is that the senator that the president commented on his ass?’ I was like, ‘Oh my god,’” Moreno told The Sun, adding that he also heard about the remark while campaigning for Mike Rogers in Michigan. “Random Uber driver, he had no idea who I was.”

Husted himself got in on the act on the eve of Trump’s planned event Wednesday evening in Chillicothe.

“Don't worry, I was in the weight room this morning working out,” Husted said to laughs from the crowd. “I don't let him down."

Trump has made his riff about Husted’s rear end part of his regular stump speech since first commenting on it at a rally in Youngstown earlier this month. On Tuesday in Texas, he compared it favorably to the appearance of Ken Paxton, the state attorney general and GOP Senate nominee whose looks he has derided.

20261028_mcgarvey_OHGOP_5483.jpg (7757x5174, AR: 1.50)Back in Ohio for another rally Wednesday night, the president again recounted how he had noticed Husted’s backside and said he changed how people look at the Ohio senator.“He took on a whole new persona. He went from — sort of like Clark Kent, if you think about it – and he became Superman.”

While Trump claimed that Husted has seen a massive polling spike as a result of the discourse surrounding his appearance, the race remains central to both party’s hopes of winning the Senate majority. Thune told Husted’s supporters in Clyde, Ohio, that the state is “ground zero” for determining control of the chamber. Republicans widely believe the incumbent senator is in a dogfight that will go down to the wire.

The Senate race is also among the most expensive contests on the map this year. According to AdImpact, more than $380 million is set to be spent on the Husted-Brown battle through Tuesday.

Ohio Republicans are quick to point to Moreno’s victory two years ago when Brown led in almost every poll until the final week, when the state’s rightward bent returned to form and Republican voters turned out to back the now-senator. Moreno won by more than 3 percentage points.

When asked if Republicans are finally coming home, Moreno said: “I think so.”

entries.title: Democrats Seek to Close the ‘Elon Musk Loophole’ in Campaign Spending
entries.summary: Chris Van Hollen and Robert Garcia want to bar the blustery billionaire and others from making campaign contributions while their companies profit from government contracts.
entries.content:
Elon Musk’s ability to influence elections could be sharply curtailed under a new proposal, shared first with The Washington Sun, that offers an early look at how Democrats might use power if next week’s elections go their way.

The idea, from Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland and California Rep. Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, is to pass a bill closing what they’re calling the “Elon Musk loophole.”

They’re referring to a facet of federal campaign law that has allowed the world’s richest man to pour nearly half a billion dollars of his personal wealth into the 2026 midterm elections, all while his companies hold tens of billions of dollars in federal government contracts.

“If you ask the normal person on the street whether it reeks of corruption for a CEO or big corporate shareholder to spend boatloads of money to elect members of Congress who will then ratify billion-dollar federal contracts, I think almost every person would say that stinks,” Van Hollen said in an interview.

“American people across the political spectrum don't want to see a Congress that's bought and paid for by Elon Musk, and the fact that he is doing that while he's raking in billions and billions of dollars of federal government contracts is rank corruption,” he said.

Current law forbids federal contractors to make any sort of donation to federal campaigns, but Musk can contribute freely because his companies — such as SpaceX and Tesla — are considered separate legal entities.

Van Hollen’s bill, which he said he plans to introduce next month, would amend the law to also ban executive office holders, major shareholders and affiliated corporations from making campaign donations.

Musk’s election spending this year has been historic and unprecedented, setting off alarms among Democrats and government watchdogs. The billionaire has given $446 million to Republican candidates and Republican-aligned groups so far, making him the Republican Party’s single largest donor this cycle.

Sign up for The Stakeout, The Sun's Congress newsletter you actually want to read. 

Nearly half of Musk’s spending has been concentrated in Texas, where SpaceX is based and develops and launches its rocket systems. He has poured about $190 million into a Republican super PAC on a mission to rescue Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton, who’s in a tight race against Democrat James Talarico that will help determine control of the U.S. Senate.

The super PAC spending is making up for the fundraising gap between Paxton and Talarico, who has raised more than any other federal candidate in this election cycle. Talarico has accused Musk of “trying to buy” a Senate seat in Texas.

“We just found out that the richest man in the world is almost single-handedly bankrolling this effort to install Ken Paxton in the Senate and defeat the movement that we are building in our state,” Talarico said at a campaign event Tuesday. “In all likelihood, if you've seen an attack ad on your TV, that was Elon. If you've gotten lies in your mailbox, that was Elon. If you've received a text message saying scary things about me with scary black and white photos, that was Elon, too."

Musk, meanwhile, has railed against Talarico on X, the social media platform he owns, calling him a "creep," "pure evil" and a "far left extremist," and posting that "there is something deeply wrong with Talarico.”

Van Hollen’s bill would not bar such activity on Musk’s own website.

Representatives for Musk did not immediately answer a request for comment.

Beyond trying to stanch the tech titan’s virtually unlimited ability to spend on elections, Democrats have signaled a broad oversight agenda if they take control of one or both chambers of Congress next month.

Already, some Democratic lawmakers are calling for subpoenaing Musk to testify about reports that he restricted or slowed Ukraine’s access to Starshield, the satellite network that Musk owns and Ukraine uses to defend against drone strikes. Democrats also have concerns regarding Musk's leadership of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) last year, and a long list of potential conflicts of interest in government.

Musk will probably also play a starring role in the crowded 2028 Democratic presidential primary, which looks set to ramp up quickly after the midterm elections.

Van Hollen, a progressive senator who is “kicking the tires” himself on a White House run, estimated that Musk, through his companies, has made approximately $20 billion in profits on taxpayer-funded government contracts.

“Even spending $450 million [on campaign contributions] this cycle, he's getting a great return in terms of taxpayer-funded government contracts,” Van Hollen told The Sun over the phone while campaigning for Democratic candidates in Georgia.

The bill has little future in the current Republican-controlled Congress, and even if Democrats win both chambers of Congress and can pass it next year, President Donald Trump, who benefits from Musk’s spending, could not be expected to sign it into law.

Still, Van Hollen said he believes his bill sends a strong message and presents the likeliest path to address the huge sums of money flooding elections, because courts have previously upheld restrictions on campaign spending by federal contractors.

He said lawmakers would not have to pursue the even more difficult path of seeking a constitutional amendment, as they would to overturn the Supreme Court’s 2010 Citizens United ruling that opened the door to unlimited corporate campaign spending.

“Federal courts have reviewed this limitation and found that it is constitutional. It doesn't violate anybody's First Amendment rights or rights to contribute, because they recognized this is clear political corruption,” Van Hollen said.
