entries.title: In a Western Massachusetts Town, Everyone Is Someone Else's Fascist
entries.summary: Fights over school funding and redevelopment projects in the deep-blue town of Northampton have taken on the ugliest traits of national politics: mudslinging, name-calling and body-shaming.
entries.content:
NORTHAMPTON, Mass. — Opponents of the mayor’s budget concluded that she hated children. The project to redevelop Main Street was denounced as racist, and the purchase of a church was compared to the handling of the Epstein files. A former city council member posted a drawing on social media of “The Mayor” next to a bomb and the caption “villainize neoliberals.”

And now came an Instagram photo from a public meeting, zoomed in on the mayor’s feet, deriding her so-called cankles, apparently engorged from “carrying the water of imperialism.”

The mayor, Gina-Louise Sciarra, a 52-year-old mom of two, really liked the burgundy sandals in the photo. They were comfy and added a pop of color. But now wasn’t the time to contemplate the contour of her leg, because a local leader was walking into her office. The mayor took a seat by the window, near the rainbow flag.

They didn’t agree on every issue, but the political gulf in Northampton isn't very wide. They were meeting to discuss things like the schools, zoning, taxes, and now, the storm of insults that had targeted them both.

Sometimes it felt like the whole town had been whipped into a vortex of hostility. Like the mayor, this leader had been called incompetent and corrupt. People accused her of being “in the mayor’s pocket.” Someone had slammed her in a group chat, and she was tired of pretending it wasn’t happening.

“She shared about my status as a domestic violence survivor, and she said she hoped my ex would finish the job of killing me,” she told Sciarra.

“I didn’t know that,” Sciarra said, her eyes welling.

“Nobody corrected her,” the woman said. “She said: ‘Why didn’t he finish the job?’”

Here, the fight wasn't along party lines. In this town of about 30,000, registered Democrats outnumber Republicans 18-to-1, and the political spectrum runs from ice blue to indigo. Eighty-one percent of them are white. They have launched a reparations commission, outlined five different types of equity on the city website, and acknowledged the Nipmuc and Pocumtuc Nations as first to the land they call Northampton.

They support abortion, which is available in town. Trans kids play school sports and use whichever bathroom they want. The town’s unofficial nickname is “Lesbianville, USA,” and even the churches fly rainbow flags. One resident said the worst insult here was labeling someone “Blue MAGA.”

Sign up for The Stakeout, The Sun's Congress newsletter you actually want to read. 

Although people here are demographically compelled to agree on most things, they fight with the language and tactics of the president they detest. Mudslinging. Name-calling. Cankle-shaming.

On the same day as a No Kings rally against the Trump administration, one of the mayor’s critics encouraged protesters to stop by City Hall: “We’ve got a dishonest democracy-disdaining demagogue usurping power, overstepping authority, unilaterally governing, and demanding fealty modeling monarchy in our very own backyard.”
20260923_Picture_Main_St_Editorial-48.jpg (9687x4778, AR: 2.03)20260923_Picture_Main_St_Editorial-196.jpg (6321x4214, AR: 1.50)Nationally, politics has gone rancid. Civility is plummeting, violence rising. But when the language and tactics of national political warfare filtered into this small town, it felt invasive and sinister. The issues here were personal, and the targets more exposed.

The mayor of Northampton had a staff of five, no communications manager, no security team. When she got threats, she forwarded them to the police, just like everyone else.

Sciarra didn’t tell the local leader about the odd strips of paper wheat-pasted on the front porch of her home, where she lives with her husband, two teenage daughters, two cats and a rescue dog, Nova. She realized whoever did this must’ve snuck onto the lawn after dark. She stopped hanging out on her porch.

“This feels so dangerous,” Sciarra said.

“I'm really surprised how off the rails it has gotten,” the local leader said. “In a community where you actually have so much in common, just like, on paper. How is that happening?”
* * *
Sciarra saw the pink bike with training wheels parked at the rack. It was 2019, and she was celebrating the opening of an affordable housing project.

After all the meetings and debates, a family now lived here. This bike belonged to a kid who had a new home and a safe place to play. She thought: “This is why we do this.”

And while she was on City Council, they passed a resolution declaring that Northampton welcomed refugees, and Catholic Charities of Springfield later selected her town to resettle 51 Syrians and Iraqis.

“Things like that hooked me,” Sciarra said. She’d stayed in Northampton local government for more than a decade, rising to council president before becoming mayor.

She had watched her colleagues decide not to run again and sometimes wondered if she should have done the same. She barely won reelection, and she wasn’t sure if she was the leader who could heal a community that felt so broken.

She kept reminders around her office of why she’d wanted this job. In framed photos, she poses with Sen. Elizabeth Warren, Al Gore, the Obamas.

A sticker of Taylor Swift in all her eras is taped to the bottom of her computer screen. While driving to a particularly contentious public meeting, she blasts “...Ready For It?” from her car speakers and sings along: “Baby, let the games begin.”

Critics come with the job, but the attacks on her integrity hurt. She has been stoic at public meetings; her mom taught her to never let people see her rattled. In the privacy of her office, she cried.
20260923_Picture_Main_St_Editorial-399.jpg (5968x3979, AR: 1.50)Across the country, local officials from both parties have installed home security systems as minor differences mushroomed into major conflicts. In Michigan, members of the Tyrone Township Board faced threats of death and rape this summer after a rumor spread about plans for a data center. City council members in Conroe, Texas, faced harassment and death threats after a vote related to Flock cameras. Last week, the mayor of Madison, Wisconsin, a Democrat, announced she would not seek reelection because of personal attacks, conspiracies and threats. “The price of serving,” she wrote, “has become too high.”

In Northampton, Josh Silver, a local political consultant, helped found a nonprofit to share basic facts about city government. He said policy disagreements have warped into a grand fight against the perceived establishment.

“It’s just people literally disagreeing on what good policy is,” he said. “The circular firing squad of the left is on display in Northampton as vividly as anywhere in the country right now.”

At first, Mayor Sciarra loved Northampton's nerdy engagement over the exact width of a curb and whether they really needed another bike lane. Northampton was within the “Five Colleges” area, where nearly two-thirds of residents had college degrees. Neighbors disagreed using philosophical arguments about neoliberalism and dug into city documents to find data.

People here were so equity-minded that one childless resident created a 10-slide presentation after learning that some parents slip their kids an extra $10 for snacks or arcade games at a parks and rec program.

This, that person wrote, created a “Tiered System of Citizenship.”

The mayor had started a policing alternative, the Division of Community Care, that staffed unarmed public health professionals to respond to people in crisis. She’d launched a climate action department and reduced energy use in municipal buildings by nearly 20%.

She’d boosted the school budget but said she was limited in how much she could allocate because of other municipal needs, as well as a statewide cap on property taxes that impacts available funds. Some dismissed that as an excuse.

The city spent more than $3 million to convert a church into a hub for homeless services, only for those plans to reach a standstill after federal grant options vanished under the Trump administration. Her critics called it the “churchase,” pointing to an independent appraisal that found the city overpaid by as much as $1.5 million.

Sciarra was used to those kinds of criticisms — not the cruel, righteous tenor taking over town.
20260923_Picture_Main_St_Editorial-117.jpg (5684x3789, AR: 1.50)20260923_Picture_Main_St_Editorial-133.jpg (6534x4356, AR: 1.50)At city council meetings, Dan Breindel, a former mayoral candidate, called the planning director an “authoritarian leader” who had “subverted democracy as often as physically possible.” He blamed her for potholes, dead birds and “anything you can think of that's wrong with this town, including cutting my daughter's vegetable garden.”

Breindel created a Halloween poster last year that referred to Gina-Louise Sciarra as “Giant Louse Scary Mayor” who feeds children to monsters.

His critiques were policy-driven, Breindel said, not personal. He’d created spooky lawn signs as a parody of campaign imagery, featuring a werewolf candidate with the last name Wolf. He remixed his own mayoral sign to say “Mayor of the Damned.”

“Months later, somebody told me, ‘Oh, yeah, you put up that really controversial thing where you called the mayor fat.’ … And I was like, ‘What are you talking about?’” he said. "Anytime I do anything playful or silly or jokey, there is a very loud response.”

Sciarra’s opponent in the last election, Jillian Duclos, knew and respected the mayor. They’re both moms. When people complained about Sciarra, she’d pivot the conversation. But that cost her support, she said, from “people who wanted me to be mean.”

“We're a very intellectual community, but … this is about how people feel, not necessarily what the data says,” Duclos said. “We're in this polarized place of right or wrong, black or white. It doesn’t work that way.”

Duclos came within 79 votes of becoming mayor. She did not ask for a recount.

Many people had lost trust in the mayor. They wanted the city to pay for basics before investing millions in a Main Street redesign, and said the mayor never owned up to the flawed hub for homeless services. Hand-wringing about civility, they argued, was just a way for those in power to dismiss dissent.

Two residents sent The Washington Sun a bingo card spotted in the Planning Board office that poked fun at critics with squares like: “Trying way too hard to prove how liberal they are,” “Refers to vacant lot as ‘green space’” and “FREE SPACE: I’m not racist.”

In her inaugural address, Sciarra had implored people to disagree with kindness and joy. Her remarks were dismissed as "toxic positivity” and compared to “The Handmaid’s Tale.”

Some supporters wanted her to build a social media presence like New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Do walk-and-talk videos. Reach people where they are. But she’s always felt uncomfortable in front of the camera.

“I’m a workhorse, not a show pony,” she’d tell them.
20260923_Picture_Main_St_Editorial-83.jpg (5597x3732, AR: 1.50)Sciarra tried to address the complaints in a way that felt true to herself. She heard criticism that she wasn’t accessible, so this year she started office hours for residents. She launched a wonky volunteer committee to dig into city finances.

But she couldn’t control what her teenage daughters were hearing. Sciarra didn’t know if they had seen the cankles post or the other caricatures that portrayed their mom as cartoonishly round.

She didn’t want them to grow up with the messages she received as a girl — that a woman’s worth correlated to her dress size, especially in an era of weight-loss drugs and deepfakes.

“It's really painful that now, publicly,” Sciarra said, “people are talking about my body.”

* * *

One of the people questioning the mayor’s integrity on Facebook was standing in the frozen-food aisle. So was the mayor’s husband.

Bill Scher, Sciarra’s husband, had never talked to this man in person and thought this Stop & Shop sighting was his chance. Michael Stein was on the local school committee and had asked on Facebook if “GL is lying or incompetent?”

Scher would later say he hadn’t planned to raise his voice.

His wife was a political figure, duty bound to put up with some level of dissent. But she was also the girl he met in high school when they acted together in “The Pigman.” She was the mom who always stayed behind at PTO meetings to put away the chairs.

At some point, Scher started to yell.

Stein knew this intense emotion must come from how much Scher loved his wife, but he really didn’t care whether she was, privately, a wonderful person. He had been part of the majority on the school committee who voted in favor of a massive increase in school spending. The mayor, who had final say, disagreed. He didn’t plan to back off. Stein later said in an interview: “It’s never about anything except her feelings.”

A 77-year-old woman overheard the January grocery store argument and was so alarmed that she posted a recap on NextDoor: I “told the shouter that he was frightening me. The shouter told me that ‘he can do and say what he wants.’”

Then: “IT WAS THE MAYOR’S HUSBAND.”

Scher was called “an embarrassment to feminist men.” He had “accosted” someone in an act of "patriarchal violence.”

The night after the incident, Scher put on a gray hoodie, walked to the lectern at a public meeting and read an apology from his phone: “I let my emotions get the better of me.”

During that same meeting, a former city council member stepped to the mic.

Her name was Quaverly Rothenberg. Some people affectionately called her Q. Others labeled her supporters a Qult.

She was also suing the city and three council members for censuring her last year, arguing their actions were defamatory and violated her freedom of speech.

This night, Rothenberg compared Scher to the ICE agent who shot and killed Renée Good in Minneapolis. Scher, she said, was “abusing a dissenter.”

Soon after, the Boston Globe wrote about Northampton: “The liberal Western Mass. city where the left is eating its young — and old.”

* * *

At a community cookout last month, it seemed obvious to pretty much everyone that the mayor’s administration kept making the wrong choices.

“Did you come here for politics? Did you come here for the community?” Quaverly Rothenberg asked. People paused their conversations and put down their forks.

Those in power were making decisions that she deemed dangerous. The very wealthy kept tricking liberals into believing they care about human rights, climate and homeless people.

The mayor, Rothenberg said, wanted to raise taxes. She would pretend it was for schools and sidewalks, then put the surplus toward projects like Picture Main Street, a downtown construction plan projected to cost $17 million more than its initial estimate.

The mayor and her supporters should be scared, Rothenberg said.

“We're going to storm that castle. We're going to get our government back,” she said. “If that doesn't work, we're going to see if we can get this woman taken out of office. If that doesn't work, guess what? Elections are just around the corner. We'll take her out ourselves. We'll take the whole council out ourselves."

The crowd erupted in applause.

“This is just a battle for human decency, and we cannot ask nicely for this.”

In the room were parents who felt the school system had neglected their special needs kids and people who thought the city spent too little on education and too much on Picture Main Street.
20260923_Picture_Main_St_Editorial-151.jpg (5991x3994, AR: 1.50)Michael Kane, who has been part of a group concerned about the Main Street redesign, left before the speech. Although their concerns overlap, he finds Rothenberg’s language offensive. A couple years ago, his group asked Sciarra to pause Picture Main Street, but she wasn’t interested in making changes.

“It’s hard to communicate and hard to grasp on some level how dispiriting it can be,” said Kane, who has lived in Northampton since 1980. “We need more sanity and we need to fight this and struggle ahead on the basis of principle and intelligence rather than name-calling and mudslinging.”

Online, Rothenberg had been posting photos emphasizing her own breasts as a way to expose more people to her arguments: “No OnlyFans, just an OnlyRants about the mayor of my city.”

The comments rolled in:

“I have a political revolution in my pants.”

“Northampton mountains right there.”

She’d used gimmicks before — posting videos depicting herself as a talking toilet-paper roll and showing up virtually to city council with a Zoom filter that portrayed her as a cat. She’s called the mayor and another elected leader "total fascists.”

Days after the cookout, Rothenberg posted a photo with one of her children, showing this Washington Sun reporter in the background interviewing the chef.

Rothenberg alleged that the mayor sent this reporter to cover the gathering and that an editor had close connections to the mayor. This was false. Rothenberg declined follow-up interview requests.

“This is insane,” one commenter wrote. “I love it.”

* * *

It was late September and the most divisive issue on the mayor’s agenda that week was a meeting for the $43.3 million redevelopment of Main Street.

The project, for which the city would pay $11.8 million, would leverage the need to upgrade the city’s underground pipes. It would use mostly state and federal funds to make the street safer, supporters said, with clearly marked lanes for cars and bikes, wider sidewalks and shorter crosswalks. There would be wheelchair ramps, more benches and outdoor dining spaces, misting fountains and native plants.

Her opponents called it a vanity project that would hurt local businesses. They said she cared more about aesthetics than teaching children to read. A critic edited the mayor’s face onto a Soviet World War II propaganda poster.

“We could all go French farmer resistance and dump manure on the steps of the mayor’s house and City Hall,” one person wrote on social media. Another remarked that he had never seen the mayor on a bike and asked, “do they make them heavy duty enough for someone of her physical stature?”

The mayor worried this tone would discourage civic-minded people from serving in local government. The three city council members sued by Rothenberg did not seek reelection. Five of the nine school committee members last term did not run for another elected position.

“I was accused of being part of this cabal that supports the mayor and that’s part of the deep state that’s running Northampton,” said former City Council Member Stanley Moulton, a retired journalist who is a defendant in Rothenberg’s suit. “I miss the constituent work … But again, being in that sort of maelstrom of the cesspool of social media that's really uncensored and unedited, I don't miss that.”
20260923_Picture_Main_St_Editorial-328.jpg (5712x3808, AR: 1.50)Some who work closely with the mayor said they wear baseball caps to public events or avoid them altogether for fear of harassment. At least four people who were singled out online, on various sides of the issues, said they installed security cameras at their home.

Marissa Elkins, another former city council member who is also a defendant in Rothenberg’s suit, recalled sitting on Sciarra’s porch one day when a passerby cursed at them and accused them of hating kids or teachers. A school committee member posted her home address on Facebook. She stopped going to the Pride parade and began to have panic attacks whenever she went to her daughter’s band concerts.

“I didn’t run again because I was just so tired,” Elkins said. “It was just a constant onslaught of bullshit.”

Critics were finding highly educated ways to interrogate city government. Already, the records requests for 2026 outnumbered each of the last two years, climbing to 541. A local pediatrician filed 86 of them.

Dr. Melissa Maciborski, the pediatrician, did not respond to an interview request, but has spoken at public meetings about the need for transparency.

“Critical thinking, debate and questions,” she said, “are under attack in Northampton.”

It all leaves people who were drawn to Northampton's progressive cohesion grappling with an ugly division they’d rather attribute to the other side.

“Democracy is messy and my side doesn't always win,” resident Abby Spector said at a February city council meeting. Spector, often a target of the mayor’s critics, later worked with Silver and others to help found a nonprofit called the Northampton Information Hub. “I hope all of us, residents and elected officials alike, can begin by seeing good intent in the other, no matter how passionately we might disagree…If not, I fear we will just be joining Trump's project of destroying and dehumanizing those we disagree with.”

* * *

Sciarra had been preparing for this meeting for weeks — the next in a long line of community sessions about Main Street.

She had picked out her clothes days earlier, including a new, gem-toned blue blazer from ThredUp, an online consignment store. At least, she thought, she wasn’t repeating an outfit. She paired it with black pants and black slingbacks. It felt like a game day outfit to match the hours of work behind the presentation.

She put her shoulders back and mustered some confidence as she walked into the senior center. There were lemon bars in the back. She found a chair and made small edits to her remarks.

This was the kind of town where people arrived early, and she wanted to be ready.

Twenty-six people had arrived by 6:17 p.m., and 13 minutes later, it was standing room only.

All the city officials and representatives from the design company made it through their presentation. They showed a flyover video rendering of the new Main Street, including a giant chessboard as an example of public games they could add to the project. People oohed and aahed.

Afterward, the leaders split up around the room. Sciarra steadily answered questions for almost an hour, but no one called her fascist or corrupt. No one screamed.
20260923_Picture_Main_St_Editorial-376.jpg (5757x3838, AR: 1.50)20260923_Picture_Main_St_Editorial-412.jpg (5463x3642, AR: 1.50)Their questions were about parking spots, homeless people and events in the park. Two seniors from Smith College introduced themselves as fellow Smithies and asked if she’d talk to one of their classes.

“I’d be thrilled,” Sciarra said. It was the broadest smile she had all night.

By the time everyone left, the mayor checked in with the head of public works.

“That was great,” he said. “There were no bombs of any kind. No swearing.”

In the coming weeks, the oversize chessboard rendering would become the town’s newest boogeyman.

“Who plays chess?” one person wrote in a community Facebook group. “The authoritarians in City Hall are a few moves ahead of us, the opposition.” People joined a makeshift caption contest, a speech bubble superimposed on a zoomed-in photo of the mayor:

“Those disabled poors and children are spoiling my legacy!”

“F*%k them kids!”

“I’m a piggy mayor here’s my snout, tip me over and vote me out.”

The commenters agreed there was no need to be civil.

The mayor, they said, deserved what she got.

entries.title: Trump Aides Are Leaning on U.S. Firms to Accept Russian Diesel
entries.summary: Questions around the legality of accepting Russian cargoes have made the fuel a tough sell.
entries.content:
Trump administration officials are privately encouraging U.S. firms to accept Russian diesel currently crossing the Atlantic, industry groups familiar with the conversations said, despite warnings that doing so could place them in significant legal and reputational jeopardy.

At least three vessels carrying Russian fuel left for the United States in mid-October in response to President Donald Trump’s Oct. 16 executive order waiving sanctions on Russian diesel. The ships are expected to arrive the week following the midterm elections, but it’s still not clear where the fuel is headed.

U.S. firms don’t want to take on the risks that would come with buying diesel from the Russians, in part because congressional Democrats say that Trump’s order violates sanctions laws, industry officials and energy analysts told The Washington Sun.

As the Russian ships approach the United States, the stage is set for a showdown between the private sector, the administration and Democrats. It represents a key test of the president’s unilateral authority with significant consequences for national foreign policy.

“Moscow and Washington are still scrambling to find takers, but we wouldn't be surprised if the cargoes ultimately head to Brazil,” Rapidan Energy Group said in a note to clients.

"They're being very strongly encouraged by both Moscow and Washington to take these cargoes, including with steep discounts, but they're encountering a wall of resistance based on reputation and legal risks," one analyst said.

In response to a request for comment, the White House referred The Sun to the Treasury Department. A Treasury official told The Sun that the Office of Foreign Assets Control’s "general license is consistent with actions the agency has taken in the past. We are complying with applicable laws and regulations."

Sign up for The Stakeout, The Sun's Congress newsletter you actually want to read. 

Another analyst described the cargoes as having been “shopped” for weeks by their commercial owners, but still unable to get any bites from U.S. firms. Multiple sources confirmed that the diesel cargoes did not have a confirmed buyer when they were loaded onto the tankers.

Trump’s waiver came as a surprise to the oil and gas industry and left them with many still-unanswered questions about how anyone who touches the fuel can guarantee compliance with all sanctions laws, multiple industry officials said. The waiver came only three weeks after Trump signed into law a bipartisan bill that further strengthened sanctions against Russian officials and companies.

New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill is reviewing options to push back against the potential arrival of a tanker carrying Russian diesel, as questions mount over the legality of the shipments.

The Malta-flagged Agioi Fanendes, carrying approximately 40,000 metric tons of ultra-low-sulfur diesel, was initially listed as going to the Port of New York and New Jersey, with an expected arrival on Nov. 7. That tanker’s destination in publicly available vessel tracking data has since changed to “for orders,” indicating its next port of call is unspecified.

“Make no mistake: Trump's diesel deal with Putin is corrupt and illegal, and I am evaluating options to stop it from arriving at a port in New Jersey,” Sherrill told The Sun in a statement, accusing Trump of “lining Vladimir Putin's pockets at the expense of American consumers and our democratic ally Ukraine.”

House and Senate Democrats have sent letters to ports, banks and energy companies warning them that transacting the Russian diesel cargoes could expose companies to criminal penalties. With Democrats potentially poised to take control of the House and possibly the Senate in next week’s midterm elections, those letters signal that buyers of the diesel could get ensnared in congressional investigations next year.

"Everyone is trying to run as far away from this as fast as they can. Nobody wants to touch it because they're afraid of what's going to happen in the next Congressional session," one Wall Street trader said, citing conversations with top companies. "Nobody wants to get ensnared in a lengthy legal battle or what will be a series of investigations and this looks like a classic case of that."

“The problem is legal and banking. The import is permitted by executive order, but the sanctions sit with Congress, so every counterparty is asking what happens if the politics shift after the cargo lands,” said James Noel-Beswick, an analyst for Sparta Commodities.

Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Connecticut), the ranking member on the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, demanded in letters to the owners of the Agioi Fanendes and the PVT Azura, a second tanker whose destination was Norfolk, Virginia, that they reverse course rather than deliver Russian diesel to U.S. ports.

“Any company or individual thinking about purchasing Russian diesel should be aware that they’re committing a crime and that Congress is watching,” Blumenthal told The Sun in a statement. “Also, they may be held accountable by a future administration even if this one looks the other way.”

He called on the companies to disclose the sellers, purchasers, terminal operators and insurers involved in the transfer — as well as any direction provided by the Treasury Department.

While the tankers appear to be heading toward United States ports, multiple industry analysts and officials said that they expect they will likely change their final destinations to Brazil, which has purchased significant amounts of diesel from Russia since the U.S. imposed sanctions in 2022. On Oct. 27, the Russian embassy in South Africa posted that three diesel tankers are en route to the United States.

During a Wednesday television appearance, Energy Secretary Chris Wright described the diesel waiver as an effort to simultaneously get more diesel into the global market and encourage Russia to the negotiating table over the war in Ukraine.

Those geopolitical tensions are only compounding companies’ concerns. The reputational damage associated with buying Russian oil could make it hard to pass along the fuel once it is in the United States, because it may be seen as “dirty,” said one Department of Transportation official familiar with the industry.

“Of course, this would be blood money that would end up buying something to kill Ukrainians or fund other evil Russian operations around the world. If you can live with this, go ahead and pay them,” said Maryan Zablotskyy, a member of the Ukrainian parliament.

Liability for transacting on the Russian fuel could extend for years, well beyond the final years of the Trump administration, said Jeremy Paner, a sanctions compliance attorney, describing the possibility that a future president could investigate companies involved in any transaction of the diesel. “It’s not worth it,” he said.

“You have a lot of questions that are usually answered before a decision like that would be made,” one industry official said. “It kind of leaves the industry in a tough spot where you don’t really know what to make of something.”

Ukrainians feel "absolutely abused" by Trump's decision to permit imported Russian diesel and hope American firms reject the deliveries, according to Oleg Ustenko, a former economic adviser to Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Ustenko said the decision was particularly hard to take at the same time that the U.S. tells the Ukrainians not to strike Russian oil refineries even as Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians.

"My understanding is we have people who have sympathy to us in American ports, as well as some people on the business side. Those in management may not be very happy to receive these shipments," he said. "I would not be surprised if we see a kind of boycott from the side of the U.S. ports. If it happened, it would be an absolutely fantastic symbol for us."

entries.title: His Job is to Make Baseball Dreams Come True. He’s Still Chasing His Own.
entries.summary: Matthew LeCroy, the manager of the Nationals' Triple-A team, knows that his players all have the same goal: to leave.
entries.content:
You’ve seen the video. Or, rather, you’ve seen dozens just like it, maybe even hundreds by now. In this one, shot in late September, a minor league baseball team is crammed in a locker room in Buffalo, New York. The walls, ceiling and floor are lined with plastic. Matthew LeCroy, manager of the Rochester Red Wings, is at the front of the room, a bottle of champagne in his left hand, the cork fighting for its life. When he speaks, he yells. The team had a rough first half, he says, the rasp in his voice dulling down his Southern drawl.

“But you know what we did?”

The slightest pause for emphasis.

“We fought — and we ain’t finished!”And then it’s sleeting alcohol, nobody or body part spared. His players fly with the beer and champagne, colliding into one another. In the last hour, the Red Wings, the Nationals’ AAA affiliate, had clinched a spot in the International League playoffs. In four days, they would win the second-half title in Memphis. In six, they’d lose in extra innings of the Triple-A National Championship Game in Las Vegas, falling one timely hit short. For the moment, though, LeCroy was only thinking about what was right in front of him. It’s what he’s always telling his guys — to be where their feet are — but of the many limitations of the human brain, the inability to take our own advice is near the top of the list.

So for a better view, he inched away from the chaos, ceding the thick of it to younger livers. His back found a brick wall, painted white to feel like every clubhouse he’d be in during 18 years as a minor league coach. In one motion, he rubbed his face and slicked back his hair, which is white, too, making most people assume he’s older than 50. Champagne dripped off his arms. He could not, for the life of him, wipe the smile from his face. It was amazing, really, to watch these players celebrate like this, especially with all they’d gone through at what LeCroy calls the hardest level of affiliated baseball. Seven months earlier, on the first full day of spring training, he had introduced himself with that in mind, telling the same joke he does every February.

Matthew LeCroy, AAA manager. I’m the guy none of you want to meet. 

And like with any good joke, the players laughed for two reasons: because it was funny, and because it was true.

* * *
The most basic definition of AAA is that it’s the step right below the majors (and, for balance, right above AA). But that’s an oversimplification for a lot of reasons, one of which is that not every AAA player is the same-sized step from the bigs, which can make for a lot of grumbling, quiet or otherwise.

As I called around about LeCroy this month, everyone I spoke with — a handful of his former players, two of his former farm directors, Devin Pearson, the Nats’ assistant general manager in charge of player development, plus LeCroy himself — said it’s the toughest minor league level to manage. In a recent phone interview, Pearson started explaining why before I even asked a question.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

“Guys are so close to the big leagues, but at the same time they’re not in the big leagues,” Pearson said. “Matt has this unbelievable ability to get guys to give their all even when they are frustrated. That’s a unique trait.”
Matthew LeCroy (4000x2667, AR: 1.50)LeCroy, named the International League’s manager of the year in September, is as familiar as anyone with that tension. Not only has he managed in Rochester since 2021, but he appeared in 280 AAA games as a player, the last 80 of them in his final season with a major league franchise. So every spring, in his opening day meeting with his new team, he acknowledges that everyone in Rochester has the same goal: to leave. And he’s not just talking about the players, either. Sure, he got his cracks at the majors, first as a catcher for parts of eight seasons, then as the Nats’ bullpen coach in 2014 and 2015. But LeCroy still dreams of being a big-league manager, of getting the same kind of news he delivers to a handful of players each season.

You know these videos, too. In 2019, LeCroy sobbed in front of the team — and in front of a camera — while telling reliever Aaron Barrett he was going back to the majors. Barrett had recovered from a gruesome arm injury. The clip went viral, then the canon of staged call-ups kept growing. This past summer, he brought reliever Erik Tolman into his office, a camera hidden in the room. Like Barrett, Tolman had dealt with a grisly injury that derailed his career.

At one point, he wondered if doctors might amputate his right foot, let alone whether he’d pitch again.

LeCroy, always game to act a little, asks Tolman if he’s interested in throwing in winter ball. Tolman responds earnestly, saying he would be open to it but hasn’t given it much thought. Then someone else tells Tolman it might be hard to play winter ball after he pitches in Texas. LeCroy asks Tolman if he knows where the big league team is at that moment. Tolman, grinning now, asks if they are in Texas to face the Rangers. They are, of course. Tolman starts to laugh, dropping his face into his hands. LeCroy claps from behind his desk, then stands up to hug him.

“Way to go, kid,” LeCroy says. “I’m proud of you, man. Awesome.”

It’s one of the best parts of the job, telling young men their lives have changed, that all their hard work led to what they prayed it would. And when LeCroy is doing that job well, he’s sending player after player to where he also wants to go.

“I realize I have a role here, and that’s to help guys maximize their skillsets,” LeCroy said. “So I don’t view it as … look, I know it’s a goal for me to go to the big leagues. The dream is to manage there at some point. But that doesn’t take away from what I love doing, which is exactly what I am doing right now. I believe that if I pour into that and do it to the best of my ability, I am going to get rewarded somehow.”

* * *

LeCroy’s major league call-up wasn’t as cinematic. At the end of spring training in 2000, the Twins had three catchers and then they had two, LeCroy included. Tom Kelly, the Twins’ manager, told LeCroy he had made the team. Recently married, LeCroy called his wife, Holly, who he’d met in sociology class at Clemson. He then made sure his family all had tickets to see his debut in the Metrodome.

“No cameras or anything for my reaction,” LeCroy said. “There wasn’t much internet back then. There certainly was no social following to think about.”

LeCroy was a first-round pick who had thrived in the upper minors. But by mid-June, LeCroy wasn’t hitting and got sent down. It was a harsh introduction to the shuttle between the majors and AAA. What he took away from it was how honest everyone was.
Matthew LeCroy Twins (1932x2288, AR: 0.84)After six seasons with the Twins, LeCroy signed a minor league deal with the Nationals in 2006. His knees were worn down. His arm, too. But in late May, he was starting for the Nats because of injuries to the other catchers. And in a game against the Astros, he allowed seven stolen bases while fumbling behind the plate, which only stopped when manager Frank Robinson removed him mid-inning. Worried he had embarrassed LeCroy, Robinson cried in his postgame news conference, saying: “It’s just a move that, at the time, I felt like I had to do.”

Around that time, Bob Boone, then an executive with the Nationals, asked if LeCroy was close to retiring. Boone wanted LeCroy to start managing in the minors for Washington. Feeling like he may have had a tiny bit left, LeCroy kept going, spending most of the next season in AAA with the Twins and then the next one playing independent ball in Lancaster, Pennsylvania. But that was the end of the line for him.

On the drive home to South Carolina, he called Holly and told her he was finished. Then he called Boone, who would eventually hire him to manage the low-Class A Hagerstown Suns in 2009. In Hagerstown, the ballpark was ancient, the uniforms were itchy and the clubhouse bathrooms smelled like sewage. But LeCroy viewed the situation as if he were still a player: If they won, he would rise — and rise quickly — all the way to a major league dugout.

Instead, Hagerstown went 56-78 and LeCroy was miserable. He had no control over the roster. He thought about quitting, about heading home for good, figuring he could take his credits as an education major and become a superintendent. At the end of the season, right before he steered his GMC Sierra toward South Carolina, he called Holly to complain some more.

“I’m hearing a lot about you,” she told him. “You're done playing. It's about the kids now.”

“And for me it was like: ‘Man, you’re right,’” LeCroy said years later. “The truth hurts, but she saved me and made me into a soldier for these players, for this organization.”

* * *
LeCroy tells two stories about Juan Soto.

The first: When LeCroy was managing in AA Harrisburg in 2018, Soto arrived after making quick work of the previous levels. Mike Rizzo, then the Nationals’ GM, told LeCroy that, barring any unforeseen developments, Soto would spend the rest of the season in Harrisburg. After a few days, LeCroy heard that Soto was sleeping on an air mattress in an apartment with a few other players. But after LeCroy called around about getting Soto his own place, the 19-year-old stopped by his office, saying not to worry about it because he wouldn’t be in Harrisburg long. That wasn’t how Rizzo had described it to LeCroy. And yet after eight games with the Senators, Soto was on his way to the majors, never to return.

The second story: In one of those eight games, LeCroy benched Soto for not running hard to first.

“He creates a loose, family-type atmosphere in the clubhouse and has a lot of fun with the guys,” said Jake Alu, who played for LeCroy in Rochester for parts of three seasons. “But he has a presence, too, like an intimidating presence, that we’re going to get things done the right way. Everyone loves him, but they’re also a little bit scared of him at the same time.”

Since that start in Hagerstown, LeCroy has hit every step of the minor league ladder, spending a year in high-A, six in AA and the last six in Rochester. His staffs have turned over. His bosses have changed.

But last fall, when the Nats’ new front office was deciding who to retain, Pearson wondered if LeCroy would buy into their vision. They planned to overhaul the entire player development operation, putting data at the forefront. LeCroy, on the other hand, was just about an organizational lifer, used to doing things a different way.

Yet once they met with LeCroy, any concern vanished. “The whole way he handled himself was: ‘I just want to learn, I just want to be a part of this,’” Pearson recalled. “I was shocked, to be honest, the first time I talked to him about how open he was to what we were doing.” They didn’t need LeCroy to speak in new-age baseball talk, either. They needed him to be himself while serving as a coordinator for the whole AAA level.
Matthew LeCroy (4000x2667, AR: 1.50)From 2 to 6 p.m. every day, that meant overseeing detailed, individualized training plans for every player. From 6 p.m. on, it meant managing the games. At all hours, he had to be on top of the nonstop roster churn, as the Nats were often sending players to and from Rochester to aid their struggling bullpen. The Red Wings rostered 80 different players in six months. They also won 90 games in the regular season, the most of any minor league team.

“The only constant in AAA is change,” said Dan Mason, Rochester’s longtime general manager. “It can be really hard to win without any consistency, but he just kept figuring it out.”

* * * 

It’s a busy week in the LeCroy house, as it is at the end of every October. In 2004, they bought in Belton, South Carolina, a half hour south of Greenville. Right before their first Halloween, their neighbor told LeCroy he’d better be ready for a lot of kids, so LeCroy bought a good bit of candy. He was sure it was enough. But then they were streaming into his yard, one wave after another. He rushed to the store to get more bags.

From then on, the LeCroys made Halloween their thing, a kind of annual thank you to the community that raised him. LeCroy grew up in Belton, his dad working in a textile mill like many of the men there. Around the turn of the century, though, some of the mills started closing, making the place “go down in the dumps,” as LeCroy put it. A big Halloween felt like the least he could do, especially with how closely the town had followed his career.

He and Holly bought a popcorn machine. One year, when a little kid got only one piece of candy, LeCroy heard him say to his dad: “I thought you said a major league player lived here.” Everyone got handfuls after that, no exceptions. LeCroy estimates that they see as many as 2,500 trick-or-treaters, spending up to $2,000 on candy to make sure they never run out again.

His five kids love it, always inviting their friends over for a big meal. But no matter how many times they’ve told their dad to dress up, he never puts on a costume. The night is about everyone else.

entries.title: Crypto Went Big for Republicans After Democrats Sank the CLARITY Act
entries.summary: The industry network directed $69 million to support the GOP, heavily boosting Ohio Sen. Jon Husted.
entries.content:
After Senate Democrats blocked legislation backed by cryptocurrency groups in September, the industry’s major super PAC network reiterated plans to remain a bipartisan group supporting pro-crypto candidates on both sides of the aisle.

They’ve mostly failed.

Federal Election Commission filings show that the crypto industry’s main political action committee, Fairshake, spent on behalf of parties about equally since Sept. 1. The super PAC spread more than $3 million among Democratic Reps. Janelle Bynum of Oregon, Steven Horsford of Nevada and Derek Tran of California, with a similar amount going to Republican Reps. French Hill of Arkansas, Bill Huizenga of Michigan and Bryan Steil of Wisconsin.

But when it comes to broader spending by its network, Fairshake has overwhelmingly helped Republicans. In fact, since that failed vote on Sept. 15, Fairshake has transferred money only to its campaign affiliate that helps the GOP, while delivering no new funds to its linked group backing Democrats, according to data available through Oct. 14.

The Fairshake PAC, whose major contributors include Coinbase, Ripple and Andreessen Horowitz, transferred $69 million to the Republican-focused affiliate, Defend American Jobs. It did not move any money to its Democratic affiliate, Protect Progress, between Sept. 1 and Oct. 14, FEC filings show.

Defend American Jobs has deployed around $66 million this fall to prop up incumbent senators who supported the CLARITY Act, with the vast majority — more than $55 million — going to support Ohio Republican Sen. Jon Husted and defeat former Sen. Sherrod Brown, a crypto nemesis whom the industry helped boot from office in 2024.

Protect Progress was transferred no new funding from Fairshake, but it did spend $2.5 million to boost Democratic House candidates, primarily incumbents, among them Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar, ranking Budget Committee member Brendan Boyle and California Rep. Jimmy Panetta.

Sign up for The Stakeout, The Sun's Congress newsletter you actually want to read.

Colin McLaren, the head of government relations at the crypto advocacy organization Solana Policy Institute, said this fall’s crypto investment has been the industry’s reaction to the halted bill.

“The opportunity that was presented back in September was a real opportunity for incumbents that may have been in tough races to demonstrate their position on the issue,” McLaren said. “At the end of the day, when you look at the map and you look at how votes fell, you can see how groups like Fairshake interpreted it really clearly.”

The spending against Brown recalls his previous Senate run, when the industry spent $40 million to oust the crypto critic from his seat and his role as the Senate Banking Committee chair.

The Fairshake-affiliated group also waded into a new Senate race in deep-red Nebraska in October. Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts, who supported the industry-backed bill, is facing a tough challenge from independent candidate Dan Osborn, whom the crypto network has spent more than $11 million opposing.

Every Senate Democrat opposed the vote to advance the CLARITY Act, citing ethics concerns related to President Donald Trump. The vote called into question the industry’s support for Democratic senators such as Ruben Gallego of Arizona and Elissa Slotkin of Michigan, for example, who each received $10 million from the industry during their 2024 campaigns.

McLaren said the electoral map influenced where crypto groups directed their spending this year. He pointed to the fact that Gallego, Slotkin and other pro-crypto Democrats like Sens. Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland and Kirsten Gillibrand of New York, who helped negotiate the CLARITY Act, are not on the ballot this year.

“There really are some fantastic pro-crypto Democratic senators,” McLaren said. “Sadly, those senators aren't in any sort of battleground seats right now … The direction is forward, and those relationships need to keep being built.”

McLaren said that the industry has maintained its promise to support lawmakers in both parties who are supportive of the industry. The CLARITY Act passed the House on a bipartisan basis more than a year ago, with 78 Democrats joining Republicans to advance the measure.

Still, data from OpenSecrets indicates that the crypto industry is undergoing a longer-term shift by party. In 2022, crypto-affiliated political spending groups actually favored Democrats, spending $28 million for Democratic candidates and $2 million against Republicans while shelling out just $16 million for Republicans and $1 million against Democrats.

Those groups reversed course in 2024, spending $48 million for Democrats and $1.5 million against Republicans while funding $69 million for Republicans and $13 million against Democrats. The partisan gulf widened sharply this year –– in 2026, crypto-affiliated groups spent just $31 million for Democrats and nothing against Republicans while spending $82 million for Republicans and $40 million against Democrats, according to the OpenSecrets data.

“In the 2022 cycle, the first one where they were really active, they actually spent more for Democrats than for Republicans,” Andrew Mayersohn, who researches committee spending at OpenSecrets, said. “Whereas this cycle, they've spent more than twice as much for Republicans as for Democrats.”

McLaren said that shift isn’t surprising to him since Republicans have historically been more supportive of the industry’s growth. But, he added, crypto groups want to maintain relationships on both sides of the aisle while control of the next Congress and the party of the next president remains to be seen.

“It’s understandable that there might be a slight bend towards Republican incumbents, particularly given the fact that that has traditionally been the standard-bearer for the industry on these issues, but we are open for that to change,” McLaren said. “We want this to be a nonpartisan issue, not a right or left issue.”

entries.title: Talk to Tom: How to Get a Reservation at Albi
entries.summary: Plus: Recommendations for a 10th anniversary dinner and where to eat in Dublin.
entries.content:
Welcome to Talk to Tom, the dining-advice column that aims to point you toward good meals, steer you from the dross and solve your pressing restaurant queries. Look for a fresh Q&A every Thursday in this space.

Questions and comments can be submitted to TalkToTom@washingtonsun.com. Submissions may be edited for length and clarity.

Now that everyone and their mother has glowingly reviewed Albi in Washington, how is a mere mortal supposed to get a reservation? 

“Truth is,” texts William Simons, the director of operations and wine director, “it’s the same as it ever was, really. If people plan ahead and try when the reservations window opens, there are generally spots open.” For December, the window opens at midnight Nov. 1, for example.

The Palestinian restaurant, launched in the Navy Yard in 2020 by chef Michael Rafidi, was my No. 1 pick in my last annual dining guide for The Washington Post, a rating my predecessor gave the establishment earlier this month. In June, The New York Times awarded it four stars — its highest rating ever for an out-of-Manhattan review. Two years ago, Rafidi won the James Beard Award for outstanding chef in America.

Simons says that it “helps to be open to times out of the prime-time rush and non-weekends” and guides wanna-be diners to the notify list on Resy. “When we see cancellations, they’re generally two days prior to the date which will open the occasional last-minute spot.”

A friend who went twice recently says his second dinner was easier to access when a pal booked Albi’s (covered and heated) Garden Table, available for groups of 10 to 14, and promptly rounded up a posse to fill the seats. “Meal was fabulous,” reports my discerning friend. “They’re cooking beautifully.”

What now-shuttered D.C. restaurants do you miss the most? 

I appreciate this question, and not simply because it offers a stroll down memory lane. Washington benefited greatly from dozens of restaurants that no longer exist but helped put the city on the national culinary map.

High on my list would be Komi in Dupont Circle, the starry modern Greek restaurant from chef Johnny Monis; Yanyu in Cleveland Park, to my taste the best source of Peking duck, carved tableside, ever in D.C. proper; Kinkead’s, the top-notch seafood purveyor from chef Bob Kinkead in Foggy Bottom, so popular it once had a dedicated telephone number just for people soliciting charitable donations; Michel Richard Citronelle in Georgetown, the glam underground oasis with visionary Michel Richard, a trained pastry chef, in the glass-fronted kitchen; Zuki Moon, the pan-Asian dining room within a ticket’s toss of the Kennedy Center and helmed by the forward-thinking Mary Richter; and Palena from former White House chef Frank Ruta, whose combination a la carte restaurant and tasting room in the rear addressed the different wishes of his fan club. (A lot of us considered Ruta’s hamburger and roast chicken to be best in class.)

Going back even further, there was Sichuan Garden on 19th St. NW, starring master chefs from China, and Red Sage, with its then-trendy Southwestern menu and simulated thunder and lightning design. (You read that right.)

I was too young and too poor to afford the Watergate Hotel's legendary Jean-Louis Restaurant, but my predecessor at The Washington Post, Phyllis C. Richman, told me the French chef Jean-Louis Palladin, whom she called "perhaps the most famous French chef in America," made her career in its heyday in the ’80s and ’90s.

You’re celebrating your 10th anniversary. Where do you go?

The 10th is a milestone, traditionally represented by tin or aluminum — symbols of resilience and strength.

I’d spring for a restaurant with some nice age on it. The well-regarded Centrolina and The Dabney represent the class of 2015 and offer Italian and Mid-Atlantic flavors, respectively. But they’re babies compared to some of the area’s longer-lived establishments: Obelisk in Dupont Circle, Perry’s in Adams Morgan, the Bombay Club near the White House, Il Pizzico in Rockville, La Ferme in Chevy Chase, L’Auberge Chez Francois in Great Falls and the fabled, nearly-50 Inn at Little Washington in Washington, Virginia.

The most senior of the bunch, though, is Old Ebbitt Grill, whose revolving door never seems to stop and whose hospitality remains something to emulate even at … 170 years.

Do you consult with anyone on food from cultures with which you’re not super-familiar?

One of the advantages of living in a world capital is access to a lot of smart, well-traveled, discerning residents. At this point in my career, I’ve been fortunate to travel widely around the world, but if I ever had a question about, say, the food in Singapore or Brazil, I know I could reach out to someone from an embassy, or a representative from the World Bank or the Peace Corps, for an answer. Also, there are knowledgeable chefs and cookbook authors, here and elsewhere, I might contact.

Even now, I like to invite people from different parts of the world to join me in a meal that might offer them a taste of home. And I never take a Lyft or Uber where I don’t ask anyone who says they’re from Ethiopia where they go for their native food. Their answers vary widely, which makes me frustrated, in a good way: I don’t think I’ll ever be able to try them all, much as I aim to. (I love Ethiopian cooking. Right now, Beteseb in Silver Spring is a favorite.)

My wife and I will spend three nights in Dublin next month. Do you have any favorites there?

My two, tried-and-true picks share literary connections. One is the casual, long-running Winding Stair, named after a Yeats poem and located above a bookshop. Picture (very good) Irish comfort food, a chalkboard menu and a cozy dining room whose windows overlook the River Liffey.

The other is the luxe, Georgian-style Chapter One, tucked in the lower level of the Writers Museum on Parnell Square. While the top chefs have switched since my last visit, Chapter One’s menu continues to highlight prime Irish ingredients — Clare Island salmon, Donegal lobster, roast pigeon — using French techniques. Don’t say good night before sampling the best Irish coffee anywhere. The signature drink is prepared tableside by a server who pours a spiced syrup into a hot pan, caramelizing the sweetener. Brazilian coffee, whiskey finished in beer barrels, and a finish of whipped Irish cream complete the dream.

I haven’t been, but food pals sing the praises of the historic, Art Deco gastropub Davy Byrnes and the refined Sole, acclaimed for its seafood.

entries.title: Hegseth Fires a Top Military Strategist Over Alleged Classified Leaks
entries.summary: The Pentagon says Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia failed three polygraph exams and has been referred to the Justice Department, escalating a sweeping leak hunt.
entries.content:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has fired Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia, the Pentagon's top military planner, amid allegations that Sylvia leaked classified information to reporters.

Sylvia was abruptly removed this week as director of strategy, plans and policy on the Joint Staff, an influential position that coordinates military planning between Pentagon leadership, the Joint Chiefs and the White House.

His dismissal leaves the office without an announced replacement as President Donald Trump weighs renewed military strikes against Iran following next week’s midterm elections. It also marks a significant escalation in the Hegseth team’s probes into leaks, which have subjected dozens of military officers and civilian officials to polygraph examinations.

A senior Pentagon official said Thursday in a statement that Sylvia had failed three polygraph exams concerning the disclosure of classified information about the Iran war and Russia’s war in Ukraine. The allegations could not be independently verified.

“The extent of the leaking became so critical that Secretary Hegseth took immediate action and fired Sylvia in order to protect national security,” the official said. “Urgent action was needed and could not wait another second.”

The official accused Sylvia of meeting journalists outside the Pentagon to disclose classified information, circumventing new restrictions requiring reporters to be escorted while inside the building.

The investigation remains ongoing, the official said, and it has been referred to the Justice Department for further action.

In a separate statement, the Pentagon’s chief spokesperson, Sean Parnell, said the personnel action followed an extensive probe by the Air Force Office of Special Investigations. He said it was among multiple matters referred to the Justice Department for potential further legal action.

“The Department of War has zero tolerance for the intentional, unauthorized disclosure of classified information,” Parnell said. “Anyone who compromises sensitive national security information puts the lives of our Warriors at risk and undermines every military operation that keeps our country safe.”

Parnell said no further details would be provided, citing the need to protect the integrity of the investigation.

“We vowed to find you, and we meant it,” he said.

As director of the Joint Staff’s strategy, plans and policy directorate, known as the J5, Sylvia occupied an influential decision-making role responsible for developing military strategy and policy recommendations for the chair of the Joint Chiefs of Staff.

The directorate works closely with combatant commanders, civilian Pentagon officials and the National Security Council to coordinate military planning and policy.

The Pentagon official emphasized that Sylvia was not a central planner for the Iran war, saying the responsibility rests with U.S. Central Command and its chief, Adm. Brad Cooper.

The Pentagon launched a broad investigation into unauthorized disclosures after reports revealed sensitive details about the depletion of munitions stockpiles during the Iran war.

The New York Times reported in September that about 50 Joint Staff personnel underwent polygraph exams in August as investigators sought to identify the source of leaks about shortages in U.S. munitions stockpiles. That followed Hegseth’s July announcement of a joint Pentagon-Justice Department task force to probe leaks of sensitive information.

The Pentagon did not immediately respond to questions about the extent of the leak probes and whether any other officials face disciplinary action.

Before joining the Joint Staff, Sylvia commanded the Army’s 101st Airborne Division at Fort Campbell, Kentucky. He also previously served as the J5’s vice director.

Sylvia retired from the Army after being removed from the director position, which he had held for 11 months.

He is the second general forced out of the strategic planning position under Hegseth. His predecessor, Lt. Gen. Joseph McGee, was pushed into retirement last October.

Sylvia’s firing comes amid a broader shake-up of the military’s senior leadership under Hegseth.

In September, Hegseth announced that the Pentagon was cutting its senior ranks by 20%, saying roughly 10% of generals and admirals had already been let go and another 10%of general officer positions were eliminated.

“Now the media calls that a purge. I call it accountability and long overdue, and frankly, the bare minimum,” Hegseth said during a speech last month at Marine Corps Base Quantico, in Virginia.

entries.title: As Alex Ovechkin Embarks on a Farewell Tour, Another ‘Great 8’ Knows the Feeling
entries.summary: Few professional athletes get to go out on their own terms. Cal Ripken was one of them.
entries.content:
There is no evidence whatsoever that Alex Ovechkin wants or needs any outside advice on how to navigate his 2026-27 farewell tour from hockey. It shouldn’t be complicated: At his final stop in each NHL city this season, at the end of his 22-year career, his starring role is to take the ice one last time in his Washington Capitals uniform, wave to the crowd at the appropriate moment — and if the opponent happens to offer a gift at some prearranged ceremony, accept it with gratitude and humility.

But if Ovechkin, the NHL’s all-time leading goal scorer, were to be open to some well-intended, time-proven advice, he could do much worse than this:

“First of all, your priority is always to the game. Focus on the game, prepare yourself for the game. But beyond that, go ahead and let yourself surrender to it — to the acknowledgment of you and what you meant to the sport. Someday, you’ll appreciate the opportunity to bring some closure and say goodbye.”

The speaker of those words is someone who would know.

In the summer and fall of 2001, Baltimore Orioles legend Cal Ripken Jr. — who, like Ovechkin, wore No. 8 and spent his entire storied career with one franchise — undertook a similar farewell tour across MLB. Twenty-five years later, some of the specifics are a little fuzzy, but what Ripken remembers most are the sentiments he was greeted with at each stop and the emotions they evoked — even if, in the moment, he forced himself to push them aside out of a sense of duty to the game.

“You really only gain that perspective later. I’ve been out of the game 25 years now,” said Ripken, now 66. “You really start to appreciate it, how long you were able to play the game, and you consider yourself lucky. So when you’re sitting in that rocking chair — which some of the teams actually gave me as sort of a joke — and you’re thinking back, you think of it fondly. Going out [of the sport] can be a wonderful, positive experience.”

Ovechkin, 41, announced earlier this month, two days before the Capitals’ home opener, that this would be the final season of his career. For an athlete of his stature — the most prolific goal scorer of all time, and a 12-time all-star and three-time Hart Memorial Trophy winner as the league’s most valuable player — that naturally set into motion plans for a season-long farewell tour.

The first of Ovechkin’s farewells came just 12 days into the season, on Oct. 13, when the Capitals visited the Carolina Hurricanes for the final time this season, and where the acknowledgment of Ovechkin was brief and tasteful: an announcement over the public-address system and a warm standing ovation from the crowd. The next one comes Thursday night in Nashville against the Predators.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

When Ripken first heard the news of Ovechkin’s retirement announcement, his first concern was for the latter’s emotional state. Though they are only casually acquainted, Ripken understands perhaps better than anyone the fraught mental calculus involved in recognizing when the time has come to say goodbye to something that you’ve dedicated nearly your entire life to.

“Everybody has to come to grips about when it’s their time,” Ripken said. “Usually, you don’t get to decide. The game decides for you. And only a few of us have a chance to make that decision on our own. And with Ovechkin retiring, I think it’s cool that he had the chance to go out on his own terms and to be able to say goodbye along the way.”

Cal Ripken AP - 01071002749 (1992x1426, AR: 1.40)
Ripken made his own retirement decision during midseason, in June 2001, spurred in part by the Orioles’ shift to a rebuilding phase. At the time, Ripken had already laid the groundwork for his next chapter — a grassroots baseball empire that would come to include ownership of minor league teams, a youth baseball complex in his hometown of Aberdeen, Maryland, and a charitable foundation named for his father and namesake. By announcing his retirement during the season, he figured he could shift attention to those future endeavors and help promote them through the media.

“I didn’t think of it in terms of, ‘Well, I’ll get a farewell tour,’” Ripken recalled. “I just thought it might create some attention, so I could answer the question: ‘What are you going to do next?’ It’d be a perfect transition. But the byproduct of that was a pretty heartfelt opportunity to say goodbye.”

Like Ovechkin, who had just one goal through the Capitals’ first 10 games, Ripken struggled during his final season, hitting just .239 with a .637 OPS, both career lows. But he recalls a night in Miami when he homered off a 100-mph fastball from Marlins ace A.J. Burnett, prompting his awed teammates to ask, “How’d you do that?”

“And I’m thinking, ‘Well, I still have something left in the tank,’” Ripken recalled. “And it makes you think, ‘Well, if I can still do that, should I really be retiring?’”

The first of Ripken’s farewells that season came at Chicago’s Comiskey Park in early July, where the White Sox held a brief ceremony on the field and gifted him a box seat from the old Comiskey Park, which had been demolished in 1991. Less than two weeks later at theMLB All-Star Game in Seattle, after Ripken’s retirement was acknowledged with a standing ovation, he homered and earned the game’s MVP honors.

When the farewell tour resumed in the second half of the season, the gifts kept piling up: a pair of cowboy boots from the Texas Rangers, a case of wine from the Oakland A’s, a year’s supply of stone crabs from the Tampa Bay Devil Rays. There were a handful of plaques, framed photographs, four- and five-figure donations to the Cal Ripken Sr. Foundation and, yes, more than one rocking chair.

“To me, it was a little embarrassing to go through some of the formal ceremonies,” Ripken said. Much more to his liking was the reception he received during a four-game series at Boston’s Fenway Park in late September, where each of his at-bats was greeted with a standing ovation. “It was more spontaneous,” he recalled. “And it was a pure baseball thing.”

Alex Ovechkin AP - 26281016452357 (5725x3817, AR: 1.50)
One subtle yet significant distinction between Ripken and Ovechkin is the way the former transcended his sport. Baseball historians widely credit Ripken with helping restore baseball’s public standing following the 1994-95 strike, thanks to his record-breaking consecutive-games-played streak that culminated in September 1995, when he broke Lou Gehrig’s fabled record of 2,130 consecutive games. Especially in his later years, Ripken was nearly as beloved around the country as he was in Baltimore.

Ripken thus carried none of the complicating baggage that surrounds Ovechkin, whose longtime support for Russian President Vladimir Putin seems likely to mute the reception he receives around the league. Even at home, pro-Ukraine demonstrators have gathered outside Capital One Arena before games to protest Ovechkin’s support of Putin.

But Ripken’s farewell tour in 2001 was also affected by global geopolitical events. The tragic 9/11 terrorist attacks on New York City and Washington forced a one-week pause in MLB’s schedule, with those missed games tacked on to the end of the season. As a result, the Orioles’ 2001 season and Ripken’s final farewell, instead of ending at Yankee Stadium, would come to a close at Baltimore’s Camden Yards in front of the home fans.

The last of those games, Ripken’s finale, came on Oct. 6, 2001, against the Red Sox. Having gone 0-for-3 in his first three plate appearances, he was standing in the on-deck circle as friend and teammate Brady Anderson battled Red Sox closer Ugueth Urbina with two outs in the bottom of the ninth. With the crowd chanting for Ripken — “We want Cal! We want Cal!” — Anderson battled Urbina to a full count before striking out and ending a 5-1 loss. Ripken consoled Anderson as he walked past, then both of them returned their bats to the rack in the dugout.

His playing career now over, Ripken had one last duty: a farewell speech to the Baltimore faithful. He had already prepared some remarks, figuring he would have a better chance of getting through the speech without breaking down if he were reading from a script. It didn’t quite work. His words came haltingly, broken up by long pauses as he struggled to hold himself together.

“There is one question I’ve been repeatedly asked these last few weeks: How do I want to be remembered?” his speech concluded. “My answer was simple: To be remembered at all was pretty special. If I am, I hope it was because by living my dream, I was able to make a difference.”

entries.title: FBI Putting Surveillance Antennas Atop Trump-Branded Towers
entries.summary: The agency awarded a no-bid contract to a company that manages the roofs of several Trump properties.
entries.content:
The FBI’s Video Surveillance Unit is installing antennas on the roofs of Trump Plaza in New Rochelle, New York, and Trump World Tower in New York City, according to previously unreported federal contracting documents.

The FBI handed a no-bid contract to NAMSI LLC, a company that manages the rooftops of several Trump-branded properties.

The FBI categorized it with the description “Leasing of Building Space to the Federal Government by Owners.” The document describes the Trump-branded properties as “optimal antenna locations for the ACRx system in the New York City region.”

The ACRx — Adaptive Central Receive — antennas are used to pick up video-surveillance signals.

“If the FBI is unable to use NAMSI for the sites referenced above, the required technology cannot be installed on locations that have already been vetted and approved,” the documents read.

The Department of Justice awarded NAMSI a $72,525 contract for the two installations on Sept. 1. NAMSI has also received no-bid awards for other ACRx installations on non-Trump-branded properties.

The White House referred a request for comment to the FBI, and neither the FBI nor NAMSI responded to requests for comment. The Trump Organization also did not return a request for comment.

The Trump Organization stopped managing Trump Plaza, a high-rise condominium, in 2021 but continues to manage Trump World Tower, the Manhattan condo skyscraper. It’s unclear if Trump’s business organization directly stands to make money from the use of the Trump World Tower’s roof by the FBI, and if so, how much.
Trump.World.Tower (1395x2000, AR: 0.70)The FBI has had an ACRx antenna atop Trump World Tower since at least 2022, per a prior contract awarded to NAMSI.

President Donald Trump had a less-than-cordial relationship with the FBI between his two presidential terms.

In August 2022, the FBI executed a search warrant at Trump’s Mar-a-Lago resort in Florida and seized boxes of documents Trump had taken with him after departing the White House in 2021.

The special counsel investigation into Trump’s handling of the classified documents resulted in charges against him related to his retention of the documents. Florida U.S. District Court Judge Aileen Cannon, who was overseeing the case, dismissed the charges, ruling in 2024 that special counsel Jack Smith had been unconstitutionally appointed. The DOJ stopped pursuing the inquiry after Trump won the 2024 presidential election.

The Justice Department under Trump has dramatically shifted its priorities. It’s probed the president’s perceived foes and former FBI employees tied to the search at Mar-a-Lago have been subpoenaed.

The Drug Enforcement Administration has also contracted with NAMSI to use Trump World Tower for “antenna and equipment” dating back to at least 2020.

The government’s need for the new antennas atop Trump buildings dates to 2015, when the Federal Communications Commission auctioned so-called AWS-3 airwaves, raising $44.9 billion.

In doing so, it sold the 1755–1780 MHz spectrum used by the Department of Justice’s video surveillance links, forcing it to adjust its spectrum usage.

The new antennas at the Trump-branded properties “will mitigate issues caused by the AWS-3 frequency auction of 2015 to DOJ's video surveillance microwave transmission capabilities in the New York City area of operations,” per the contracting documents.

As of March, the switch was set to prompt fixes at between 35 to 45 sites, with “an anticipated six to ten installations occurring per year,” per a request for information document posted by the FBI to a federal contracting website.

entries.title: AJ Dybantsa Looked Like a Vet in His NBA Debut
entries.summary: Washington fell to the Cavaliers, 121-111, but the No. 1 overall pick finished with 19 points.
entries.content:
AJ Dybantsa’s wish came true — just not how he drew it up.

Before his NBA debut on Wednesday in Cleveland, the 19-year-old told his dad, Ace, that he wanted his first career basket to be a dunk.

Dybantsa had missed the first four regular season games after rolling his left ankle in Washington’s preseason finale, but he started against the Cavaliers while playing on a minutes restriction.

On the game’s opening possession, Dybantsa received a pass, took off toward the basket and drew a foul on his way to the rim. He had to settle for his first NBA points coming at the free-throw line.

“Just trying to be aggressive from the jump,” Dybantsa told reporters after the game. “That’s always been my game regardless of the level. I tried to punch it. I wanted my first basket to be a dunk so bad.”

A few minutes later, the rookie got his wish, catching a lob from Trae Young for his first NBA basket.

Dybantsa looked the part in his first regular season game, scoring a team-high 19 points on 8-for-12 shooting in the Wizards’ 121–111 loss to the Cavaliers. The Wizards hung with the Cavaliers — widely considered a championship contender — for most of the game. They went into halftime up 10, but lost the lead in the second half as Cleveland guards James Harden and Donovan Mitchell took over.

“We understand that we could have won tonight, could have won in Charlotte [on Monday],” Anthony Davis said. “We’re very optimistic about what we can do, what we can be. But we got to learn from these late-game situations and try to execute down the stretch.”

Dybantsa is a big reason for that optimism. Offensively, he looked like a seasoned vet on Wednesday, taking what the defense gave him and passing out of situations where he was well-covered. He made his first three shots and had 9 points and an assist in his first six minutes on the floor.

https://x.com/washwizards/status/2115613206076944424?a=hJFlgys8bI_TRgcoLbE&s=46In the second quarter, Dybantsa found Kyshawn George for a lob and later kicked out to Alex Sarr for a 3-pointer when his driving lane was cut off.

His return was welcome for a banged-up Wizards team that is now down four players. On Wednesday, the team announced that Justin Champagnie underwent surgery for a fractured foot that will likely keep him out until the All-Star break. Tre Johnson is day-to-day with a sore foot, and Tristan Vukčević (hip) and Jamir Watkins (ACL) remain sidelined. Dybantsa said after the game that he had no issues playing with his ankle.

“Feels good,” he said. “I didn’t want to come back not 100%.”

Dybantsa wasn’t the only young Wizard in a groove against the Cavs. Sarr had 13 points in the first half and Bilal Coulibaly had 14, while Dybantsa went into halftime with 11. The trio overshadowed Davis and Trae Young, serving as another reminder that the Wizards have the young talent to complement their All-Star veterans.

Dybantsa logged 27 minutes, which was “about in the range” of the restriction the Wizards played him under, coach Brian Keefe said.

Keefe put Dybantsa back in the game late in the fourth quarter with the Wizards trailing, but the rookie was unable to turn his team’s fortunes. He missed a 3 and a running layup in the closing minutes.

Even Keefe admitted that the Wizards aren’t used to playing in tight games together. But now that their main pieces are finally on the court together, they can start to learn.

“Those are the things we’re learning,” Keefe said. “We’re a new group. How we’re going to execute in those situations. It’s the first one that we’ve actually been in, including the preseason, so it’s good for us to go through this.”
