entries.title: Trump Scraps a Weekend Trip to Kansas
entries.summary: The president’s planned event with Sen. Roger Marshall has been canceled, according to a local official.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump’s Kansas campaign event with Sen. Roger Marshall has been canceled, Kasey Windhorst of the Salina Airport Authority confirmed to The Washington Sun.

The Saturday event would have included a noon speech from Trump, Windhorst said.

A White House official pushed back on the idea that the change signals trouble in Kansas, saying demand for the president’s time has outpaced his travel schedule. “Every candidate wanted POTUS to come to their districts to campaign for them. We hadn’t even left Ohio and they were asking us to come back. Standing up telerallies allows him to hit EVERYWHERE with everything tightening. There will be over 20 telerallies before Election Day,” a White House official told The Sun.

A GOP source familiar with the operation offered the same explanation, saying demand from candidates has been “huge” and the campaign is “adjusting to a tele-rally to maximize his reach and communicate with as many voters as possible.”

Marshall's campaign didn't immediately respond to questions about why the event was canceled.

It would have been Trump's second trip to Kansas for Marshall, amid a busy midterm blitz that’s taken the president largely to states he won comfortably in 2024.

Trump carried Kansas by more than 16 points two years ago, and Marshall won his first term in 2020 by 11. Democrats have not won a Senate race in Kansas since 1932.

Marshall said earlier this month that the path to the Senate majority “runs through Kansas.”

entries.title: Hacktivist Group IDs Thousands of DHS Agents Online After Massive Data Breach
entries.summary: An activist hacking group known as the Department of Peace took credit for the breach, which it dubbed operation “Icepick.”
entries.content:
An activist hacking group posted the personal information of more than 40,000 employees of the Department of Homeland Security online this week following a massive breach of the agency’s computer systems.

The incident was apparently meant to protest a recent spate of hard-line immigration enforcement efforts deployed by the Trump administration, according to a missive posted online by the group.

The online “hacktivist” group known as the Department of Peace took credit for the cyberattack. It then turned copies of the data over to Distributed Denial of Secrets, a platform known for hosting leaked information, and a Swiss online activist known as maia arson crimew.

"On July 17th, Markwayne Mullin said he was 'turning up the heat.' This is what happens to ICE when you do that," a Department of Peace spokesperson said, referencing a comment made by the DHS secretary earlier this year.

DHS acknowledged the reported breach in a statement shared with The Washington Sun.

“DHS is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively,” a DHS spokesperson said. “We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected. We will update the public when more information is available.”

The data breach, which the hackers dubbed “Icepick,” leaked the employees’ names, offices, contact information and assignments, according to an announcement posted by Distributed Denial of Secrets.

Some social media sites have taken steps to avoid further disseminating the personal information of the thousands of government employees who have been affected. Bluesky has been blocking links to the leaked information, Wired reported Wednesday.

DHS has been the target of several cyberattacks in recent months, with hackers breaching the Homeland Security Information Network, which helps the department share information with other government agencies, earlier this year.

Since the start of President Donald Trump’s second term, he has directed his administration to take a more aggressive approach to immigration enforcement efforts. The White House’s “Secure the Border” website touts the deportation of more than 2.5 million undocumented immigrants since January 2025.

But the administration's enforcement crackdown has been met with strong pushback from communities across the country.

The deployment of Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents has at times spurred deadly confrontations with undocumented immigrants and community members protesting the presence of the federal officials. An ABC News report published last month found that more than 20 people have been shot by federal immigration agents during Trump’s second term.

entries.title: National Links Trust Signs New Lease for Two D.C. Golf Courses, Excluding East Potomac
entries.summary: The agreement marks a definitive end to the organization's role at East Potomac Golf Links.
entries.content:
National Links Trust signed a new long-term lease on Wednesday to manage and operate two public golf courses in D.C. for the next 50 years, excluding East Potomac Golf Links.

The nonprofit said in a Thursday news release that its new lease with the Interior Department and National Park Service will have it manage, operate and rehabilitate Langston Golf Course and Rock Creek Park Golf.

According to the release, the National Links Trust’s involvement at East Potomac Golf Links will end on or before Nov. 15, when the course will close for a planned massive redevelopment amid an ongoing legal battle.

National Links Trust is preparing to complete major rehabilitation and capital improvement projects at Rock Creek Park Golf and will “deepen their work with community programs” at Langston Golf Course, according to the news release.

The nonprofit previously announced the long-term lease agreement in May, after the Trump administration terminated National Links Trust’s initial 50-year lease for all three golf courses in December. The nonprofit said at the time it would continue to operate the East Potomac golf course on an interim basis, The Washington Post reported.

The National Park Service will submit renovation plans for East Potomac Park to the National Capital Planning Commission in Washington by Friday, the same day Trump administration lawyers are scheduled to explain in court its plans to close the golf course for redevelopment.

The Interior Department did not respond to a request for comment.

entries.title: Comer Plans to Grill Democrats Accused of Alaska Ballot-Stacking Scheme
entries.summary: Republicans on the House Oversight Committee are seeking testimony from two Democratic operatives thought to be involved in the effort.
entries.content:
House Oversight Committee Chair James Comer launched an investigation on Thursday into an alleged scheme operated by Mary Peltola’s campaign and other Democratic operatives to recruit a U.S. Senate candidate with the same name as Alaska’s Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan.

The plot, revealed on Wednesday by The New York Times, was part of an apparent bid to siphon votes away from the incumbent senator. Ballot-stacking is widely considered to be legal and is a common tactic in Alaska, which uses ranked-choice voting and often has ballots with many candidates.

But Republicans, just days before next week’s midterm elections, are alleging that Peltola’s campaign and Alaska Democrats may have broken the law in some way by convincing the second Dan Sullivan — listed on the ballot as Daniel J. Sullivan — to run.

“Democrats are the party of fraud,” Comer said in a statement. “Knowing they can’t win on the issues, Democrats schemed to rig the U.S. Senate election in Alaska by deliberately confusing voters.”

For months, Republicans, including President Donald Trump, had said Daniel J. Sullivan’s appearance on the ballot was a ploy by the Democratic Party to help Peltola’s chances on Election Day. But Peltola, her campaign, the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and Daniel J. Sullivan have all repeatedly denied any involvement or knowledge of the scheme.

The Times spoke with sources connected to Peltola’s campaign and Democratic operatives who had knowledge of a plan to find and recruit Dan Sullivans to appear on the ballot. The effort was said to involve secretive trips to communities across Alaska and operatives making pitches to Dan Sullivans and others to enter the race, according to the newspaper.

Responding to the revelations on Wednesday at a rally, Peltola said that the entire situation was a distraction from the kitchen-table issues she is trying to base her campaign around.

“This is just another distraction. It's another diversion,” Peltola said. “Every day it's some new ‘look over here’ moment.”

Comer is demanding transcribed interviews with two individuals cited in the Times’ report: Elisa Rios, a former campaign manager for Peltola who attempted to retract her statements before publication, and Jerid Kurtz, a Democratic operative who was also reportedly involved in the efforts to recruit other Dan Sullivans.

“Chairman Comer emphasizes that if they fail to appear voluntarily, the Committee will evaluate the use of compulsory process,” a press release announcing the investigation said.

Trump told reporters on Wednesday he believes Peltola and Daniel J. Sullivan should be pulled from the ballot and prosecuted. Before the Times released its report Wednesday, the Department of Justice had already filed a lawsuit to stop the certification of the election results if Dan Sullivan, the incumbent Republican, lost the race.

Gov. Mike Dunleavy (R-Alaska) also directed the state’s Department of Public Safety to launch a probe into the alleged recruitment plot to determine whether it “violated Alaska’s laws and whether criminal charges or civil action are warranted.”

“Today’s New York Times reporting reveals disturbing new evidence of an organized effort to manipulate Alaska’s elections by recruiting candidates — including one with the same name as an incumbent U.S. Senator — to deliberately confuse voters and misdirect their votes,” Dunleavy wrote early hours of Thursday morning on X.

entries.title: Democrats Ask State’s Inspector General to Probe Politicized Personnel Practices
entries.summary: The lawmakers’ request follows The Washington Sun’s reporting that State Department officials asked nonpartisan staff about their voting history.
entries.content:
House Democrats have asked the State Department’s inspector general to investigate the agency's internal personnel decision making after The Washington Sun reported that nonpartisan foreign service officers up for promotion had been asked about their voting and political donation histories.

The requests came from Reps. Gregory Meeks (New York) and Robert Garcia (California), the top Democrats on the Foreign Affairs and Oversight committees, respectively, who said the practices violate the law and undermine American diplomacy.

“An administration can appoint political leadership and expect career employees to carry out its lawful policies,” the lawmakers said in their letter. “It cannot make a career diplomat’s voting history, campaign contributions, or perceived partisan allegiance a condition of advancement.”

The Democratic lawmakers asked the watchdog to probe whether the State Department has demonstrated any political favoritism within its career staff and if Secretary Marco Rubio, or other senior leaders, ordered or carried out politically motivated personnel actions. They also cited previous reporting from The Sun that State is pushing out senior foreign service personnel and identifying staff it has identified as politically aligned with administration for higher-ranking jobs.

After initially declining to comment on nonpartisan staff being asked political questions and telling The Sun that the department’s screening process was “not about partisan behavior but rather about executing the president’s vision for foreign policy,” State — seven hours after the story published — refuted the reporting and called it an “absurd premise.”

The Sun reported that top State officials asked candidates up for new assignments who they voted for in 2016, 2020 and 2024 and told the employees their political donation history would be examined to ensure no Democratic support.

Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said she and other relevant committees were already working to “thoroughly investigate” allegations of unlawful political favoritism.

Democracy Defenders Fund, a liberal group that has repeatedly sued the Trump administration, previously asked the State Department’s inspector general to investigate the reports of nonpartisan staff being asked political questions.

A spokesperson for the inspector general’s office said it could not confirm, deny or comment on investigative matters. The office is currently being led on an acting basis by Arne Baker after Trump fired Cardell Richardson shortly after taking office.

Subsequent to publication, The Sun has spoken to several additional individuals who have been asked questions about their political affiliations when being considered for new roles.

Simon Hankinson is a former career foreign service officer who after leaving the State Department cofounded the Ben Franklin Fellowship, a group whose members The Sun and others have reported are receiving preferential treatment for job placements. Hankinson denied that his group has won any outsized influence within the State Department but acknowledged screening for political alignment was likely occurring.

“Given that the overwhelming majority of foreign service officers are left-leaning, it is harder for a Republican president to find suitable ambassadors than it is for a Democrat,” he said. “That's just a fact of life. And so, yeah, they would probably want to look at somebody's history.”

Both the Democrats and Democracy Defenders Fund noted the political questions would violate the 1980 Foreign Service Act.

“Tying foreign service officers’ promotions to their personal political activity and voting record is outrageous and undermines the integrity of the entire State Department,” said DDF Executive Chair Norm Eisen. “Imposing an ideological loyalty test of this kind would fly in the face of the merit-based principles our foreign service was built on.”

entries.title: Maryland Woman Indicted on Charges of Defrauding D.C. Medicaid Program
entries.summary: A fraud scheme led the program to pay $109,000 for services the woman didn’t provide, the government says.
entries.content:
A grand jury indicted a Maryland woman on Wednesday on dozens of charges related to billing the District’s Medicaid program for services she did not provide while working at a behavioral health center in Southeast D.C.

Camille Aba submitted false claims to Family Wellness Center, where she worked in a support role from 2022 to 2023, leading to $109,000 in fraudulent medicaid payments, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia alleges. She faces 38 counts of fraud and theft, including 36 first-degree felonies.

The D.C. Department of Health Care Finance first probed Aba’s work during an investigation following a February 2023 shooting on a Metro bus. The department looked to determine if the suspected shooter had received help from a D.C. Medicaid provider before the shooting, according to court filings. An initial query showed Aba had notes from a session with the suspect in January and billed D.C. Medicaid for service. The day after the shooting, she changed her notes to omit details of the services she said she provided, according to a court affidavit.

A preliminary investigation found evidence Aba billed D.C. Medicaid for services she did not provide and used the same language in multiple case files, the affidavit said.

The D.C. Office of the Inspector General and the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia are conducting a joint investigation. Aba is scheduled for a status hearing in D.C. Superior Court on Dec. 16. No trial date has been set.

entries.title: Construction Firm Sues the State Department Over Unpaid Embassy Projects
entries.summary: BL Harbert International worked on more than a dozen embassies during the COVID-19 pandemic, claiming that their costs were close to $500 million.
entries.content:
A construction company is suing the State Department for $461 million in unpaid bills stemming from work it performed during the COVID-19 pandemic, claiming that the choice to not pay the charges “came from the top” of the Trump administration.

BL Harbert International sued the State Department on Oct. 28 for unpaid costs tied to 17 embassy and consulate projects, according to a lawsuit filed in the U.S. Court of Federal Claims.

“We did not want to take this step,” the President of BL Harbert’s International Group, Charles Bohn, told The Washington Sun. “We kept our commitment under extraordinarily difficult conditions. We are asking the government to keep its commitment to us.”

Some of the projects were in Ankara, Turkey; Casablanca, Morocco; Chiang Mai, Thailand; Guatemala City; Hermosillo and Mérida, Mexico; Podgorica, Montenegro; Windhoek, Namibia; and Erbil, Iraq.

The State Department told the company over the summer that it would not be paying claims attached to the projects, according to the suit.

In early 2020, BLHI’s projects were at different stages of construction, including active construction stalled by delays and the early design stage. The State Department requested construction projects continue despite the pandemic.

BLHI complied with the government’s request and kept the projects active, bearing the costs of pandemic-era construction, which rose in 2020 and 2021.

To complete the task, the company kept crews on standby, equipment in place and ordered materials at inflated prices, per the lawsuit.

“The government directed the means and methods of this work during an unprecedented global shutdown and required BLHI to stay in the field, while the government scaled back to part-time schedules, staggered shifts, and remote work,” the complaint states.

“The government did not pay, pocketed the benefit, and let the problem compound, year after year, as supply shortages, resequencing, and unresolved pricing disputes piled onto an already unpaid bill,” the lawsuit says.

BLHI is asking the court to rule on costs tied to 13 claims totaling $461,097,380. The total damages across 12 embassy program contracts exceed $500 million, according to the lawsuit.

The government directed BLHI to document costs and submit requests for equitable adjustments, which the company did for two years.

The claims were nearly settled, the lawsuit says, after a September 2025 meeting in which the government agreed to pay the company $370 million to resolve the matter.

But the government allegedly backed away from the agreement in a decision that reportedly “came from the top.”

“The Government did not issue the modifications, did not pay the entirety of this agreed amount and refused to honor the settlement it authorized and approved,” the complaint says.

BLHI has completed 50 embassy and consulate projects over 20 years with a total value over $8.2 billion.

The Washington Sun has contacted the State Department for comment.

entries.title: Judge Blocks Trump’s Work Requirement Rule for the ‘Medically Frail’
entries.summary: A district court said the rule could create “great hardship” for seriously ill people.
entries.content:
A federal judge has blocked a Trump administration rule that would have required chronically ill Americans, including cancer patients, to give additional proof they are unable to work in order to receive Medicaid.

Judge Richard Stearns of the U.S. District Court for Massachusetts sided with a coalition of Democratic states that called the Trump administration’s definition of “medically frail” — a category that is exempted from Republicans’ new Medicaid work requirements — too onerous.

Enforcement of “an unlawful definition of ‘medically frail’ may lead to the disenrollment of otherwise eligible vulnerable individuals relying on Medicaid coverage,” the judge ruled. He added that states and the public could face “potential for great hardship.”

Stearns also noted the tight timeline in which states were working to implement work requirements and said they should receive a six-month extension to determine if an individual qualifies as medically frail. The judge left the rest of the Trump administration’s rules around Medicaid work requirements in place.

The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, or CMS, didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Sign up for The Stakeout, The Sun's Congress newsletter you actually want to read. 

Republicans established Medicaid work requirements under their sweeping domestic policy and tax law, which President Donald Trump signed last year. The policy requires adults covered under the program’s expansion to complete a minimum of 80 hours of work or community-engagement activities per month or be enrolled in education part-time to qualify for Medicaid.

The new requirements are expected to impact about 18.5 million of Medicaid’s 66 million enrollees. States have been preparing to enforce the new requirements, which go into effect in January.

Patient advocates were concerned after CMS spelled out how the medical-frailty exemption would work in a rule issued in June. The rule said a condition must “significantly impair” someone’s ability to work and eventually would require confirmation from a doctor.

CMS’s original wording could have made it more difficult for people who are not considered disabled but have debilitating conditions, such as cancer or sickle-cell disease, to qualify for Medicaid coverage.

“Today’s decision is a major victory that ensures that some of our most vulnerable residents are able to continue to access the healthcare they deserve,” California Attorney General Rob Bonta said. “People with serious illnesses or disabilities should not have to worry about losing their healthcare because of work requirements or related barriers.”

When Republicans passed the Medicaid work requirements, Trump administration officials said they were seeking to minimize enrollee paperwork and ensure that those eligible for a work exemption received it while minimizing fraud.

entries.title: Justice Department Issues Subpoenas Over Alaska Candidate Controversy, AP Source Says
entries.summary: More subpoenas are expected, according to a person briefed on the investigation.
entries.content:
By Meg Kinnard and Alanna Durkin Richer

The Justice Department is escalating a criminal investigation over an Alaska Senate candidate who shares a name with the Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan, issuing a raft of new grand jury subpoenas, a person familiar with the matter told The Associated Press on Thursday.

Subpoenas seeking grand jury testimony or documents, along with records preservation demands, were issued after The New York Times reported that Democratic candidate Mary Peltola’s campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting Dan J. Sullivan Jr. as part an alleged effort to confuse voters in the hotly contested race.

More subpoenas were expected to be sent Thursday, according to a person briefed on the investigation who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to publicly discuss the ongoing probe. Neither the recipients of the subpoenas nor the number of them were immediately clear.

The Justice Department for months has been looking into allegations that Dan J. Sullivan Jr. entered the race to siphon votes from the incumbent Sen. Dan S. Sullivan.

The potential targets of the Justice Department’s investigation are unclear, but President Donald Trump earlier this week called for the criminal prosecution of Peltola and her campaign.

The new subpoenas were confirmed by a person briefed on the investigation who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to publicly discuss the ongoing probe.

Attorney General Todd Blanche in a Fox News interview on Wednesday said he wouldn’t discuss any criminal investigations, but accused Democrats of “cheating.”

“They are trying to take votes away from the incumbent, not by running an election, not by running on issues but by putting up a person with the same name,” Blanche said.

The race is among a handful of Senate contests this year expected to determine control of the chamber. Trump had previously directed his Department of Justice to sue to block certification of the Senate race should Democrat Mary Peltola defeat Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan.

Dan J. Sullivan has long denied he was running at Democrats’ behest and has said he had no contact with Peltola’s campaign. “Zero, none, zilch,” he said in June after announcing his run.

Separately, Republican Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy has ordered an investigation into Peltola, saying the newspaper's reporting “reveals disturbing new evidence of an organized effort to manipulate Alaska’s elections by recruiting candidates — including one with the same name as an incumbent U.S. Senator — to deliberately confuse voters and misdirect their votes.”

“Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections,” Dunleavy added, noting that the reporting “substantially supports” earlier findings by the state’s elections board into the matter.

Trump on Thursday cast doubt on whether Peltola would be seated in the Senate even if she won the election. “Well, you’re going to have to see what happens," the president told reporters on his way to a rally in South Carolina. "It’s hard to believe that she could even be allowed to run.”

Later, as he rallied for GOP Sen. Darline Graham, Trump said he felt Peltola “actually should be removed from the ballot and prosecuted."

Peltola’s campaign didn’t immediately respond to a message Thursday seeking comment on Dunleavy’s order. But during a campaign stop in Soldotna, Peltola, a former congresswoman, suggested the Times’ report was a “distraction” from issues such as Sen. Sullivan’s support of the war in Iran.

“This is just another distraction. It’s another diversion,” she said in a video posted online. “This is all stuff to sell newspapers. This is all stuff to get subscriptions.”

And the situation in Alaska isn't that unusual. Political parties often support extra candidates on ballots to try to pull votes from their rivals. If state courts allow it, legal experts say, the federal government has no role challenging the results.

In Ohio’s Senate race, Republicans have been tied to an effort to boost a socialist on the ballot who would pull votes from the Democratic candidate challenging Sen. Jon Husted.

On Thursday, Vice President JD Vance didn’t go as far as Trump did in calling for Peltola to be prosecuted but said he supported a probe into possible election fraud.

“I mean, she is a person who, for months now, has pretended that she has had nothing to do with the fact that they have put a fraudulent person, a person explicitly designed to confuse Alaska voters, on the ballot,” Vance told reporters ahead of a campaign trip to Texas. “She is trying to steal a Senate seat from the voters of Alaska, and it’s disgraceful.”

Earlier this year, a top state elections official ruled Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a retired schoolteacher in the small fishing community of Petersburg, ineligible for the primary ballot, concluding that his declaration of candidacy was filed “with a purpose to confuse or mislead and to thereby compromise the ballot’s fairness or neutrality.”

The case went to the Alaska Supreme Court, which ruled he was qualified to run. Alaskan voters will see “Dan S. Sullivan” identified as a “registered Republican” and “incumbent” on their ballots, while “Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.” will not have a party affiliation.

The New York Times reported that interviews, text messages and documents prepared for a potential lawsuit showed Peltola’s team aimed to coax candidates into the race, with the aim of splitting support for the GOP senator.

Asked about the reporting on Wednesday, Trump told journalists, “I think they should be prosecuted.” He earlier had posted on social media that “Peltola should suffer the Legal and Political consequences for what she has done.”

AP writer Seung Min Kim contributed to this report.

entries.title: Meet America’s Most Political Sports Owners
entries.summary: Dozens are playing major league election moneyball ahead of the 2026 midterms.
entries.content:
Dallas Mavericks owner Miriam Adelson remains queen among sports team owners when it comes to political donations.

Adelson, whose net worth is $30 billion, according to Forbes, has pumped at least $68 million into various Republican political committees across numerous federal-level campaigns during the 2026 midterms, according to a Washington Sun analysis of Federal Election Commission data.

While Adelson’s political spending remains in its own galaxy among American professional sports team owners, she’s hardly the only one to spend big this election season.
MiriamAdelson.Trump (4393x2923, AR: 1.50)More than 50 owners across top North American sports leagues — Major League Baseball, National Football League, National Basketball Association, National Hockey League — made at least one donation this election cycle.

Together, these sports owners donated at least $100 million, with Adelson accounting for nearly 70% of the giving. While Adelson’s money solely went to Republican causes, numerous owners donated to Democratic causes in smaller amounts. Some gave money to both parties, and others donated to their league’s federal political action committee, which both MLB and the NFL have.

Front Office Sports first reported some details of major league sports owners’ political spending on Wednesday.

A few owners have ties to President Donald Trump and have served in one of his administrations, including Houston Rockets owner Tilman Fertitta, who is the president’s ambassador to Italy.

In January 2025, Adelson and Fertitta co-hosted a black tie welcome reception in honor of Trump’s second inauguration. Former Education Secretary Betsy DeVos is the sister-in-law of Orlando Magic owner Dan DeVos, who donated more than $1 million to various Republican causes.

Meanwhile, the Ricketts family, which owns the Chicago Cubs, counts Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts and former Republican National Committee finance chair Todd Ricketts, as Trump-aligned members.

Adelson’s midterm donations come after giving $100 million to help reelect Trump in 2024. Her combined donations of $168 million the past two cycles is more than the team salary for five NBA teams this season.

The 81-year-old physician has also reportedly given $25 million to Trump’s White House ballroom project, according to The Washington Post. Adelson’s wealth stems from her late husband, Sheldon, a Republican megadonor who founded the Las Vegas Sands casinos and who died in 2021. Adelson inherited her husband’s fortune upon his death.

In December 2025, Adelson told reporters she would give Trump another $250 million if the president ran for a third term. A spokesman for Adelson didn’t respond to a request for comment.

“I met [Trump’s lawyer] Alan Dershowitz,” Adelson told reporters at a Hanukkah celebration. “He said the legal thing about 4 more years. I said Alan, ‘I agree with you. We can do it. Think about it.’”

Adelson bought the Mavericks from longtime owner Mark Cuban in December 2023 for $3.5 billion, but her son-in-law, Patrick Dumont, has been the team’s governor and league representative since the purchase.

Republicans Get Major Boost

Sports team owners backing Republicans are continuing to spend big ahead of the Nov. 3 election.

The Ricketts family remains big political spenders pouring over $800,000 into this midterm cycle. Their spending is divided among Laura Ricketts, the first openly gay owner in MLB history, who’s spent $320,000 on Democratic causes, and her brothers, Tom and Todd, who’ve together spent $480,000 on Republican causes.
Ricketts.Laura (5248x3589, AR: 1.46)The Ricketts siblings own the team through a trust. The media department for the Chicago Cubs did not respond to requests for comment or to confirm those donations. The associate communications director for the Chicago Stars Football Club, owned by Laura Ricketts, referred The Sun to the CEO of Culloton + Bauer Luce, a PR firm that works with Laura Ricketts directly. The firm declined to comment.

San Francisco Giants owner Charles Johnson eclipsed the Ricketts’ family contributions, giving more than $3 million. John Middleton, the owner of the Philadelphia Phillies, outspent most of the MLB ownership, but his $137,369.97 Republican spending paled in comparison to the league’s superspenders.

The NFL — and other leagues — also has several big spenders.

Jimmy Haslam III, owner of the Cleveland Browns and Milwaukee Bucks, put more than $1.4 million behind Republicans this election. Nearly a quarter of that amount went to the National Republican Senatorial Committee. The National Republican Congressional Committee received $155,500.

Jimmy Haslam outspent his younger brother Bill Haslam, owner of the Nashville Predators. Bill Haslam contributed nearly $160,000 to Republican causes, including the NRSC. A spokesman for Haslam Sports Group did not respond to a request for comment.

Rob Walton, Denver Broncos owner and heir to the Walmart fortune, divided more than $10 million among conservative causes. Walton also owns a 10% stake in the Arizona Diamondbacks, and his son-in-law Greg Penner is the face of Broncos ownership.

Seahawks owner Vinod Khosla gave more than $2.1 million to Democratic causes, with $2 million going to the Senate Majority PAC. Khosla gave smaller donations to Sen. Mark Warner (D-Virginia) and Reps. Sam Liccardo (D-California) and Bill Foster (D-Illinois) among other candidates.

Jerry Jones, owner of the Dallas Cowboys, gave more than $500,000 to Republicans. Half of the donation went to Paxton Victory, a political committee backing Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton in Texas.

Atlanta Falcons owner Arthur Blank has contributed $312,000 to Democratic political causes. Miami Dolphins owner Stephen M. Ross spent $130,900 in a bipartisan fashion. And Los Angeles Chargers owner Dean Spanos gave $108,500 to Republicans.

New Orleans Saints and Pelicans owner Gayle Benson poured $105,500 into midterm campaigns, with $40,000 going to committees connected to Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-Louisiana), who lost in a primary earlier this year.

Over at the NBA, Adam Silver, the league’s commissioner and a Duke University alumnus, aimed his spending at North Carolina, donating $20,000 to the Cooper Victory Fund — a committee tied to Roy Cooper — and $5,000 to the North Carolina Democratic Party. Silver is a longtime Democratic donor and gave another $16,000 to other Democratic congressional candidates.

While the DeVos family behind the Orlando Magic can’t knock Adelson’s crown as the biggest spender, the family is still a political spending dynasty in their own right.

Four members of the DeVos family — Dick, Dan, Doug and Pamella — together spent more than $4 million to boost Republican midterm efforts at the federal level. This includes $1.5 million to the Senate Leadership Fund and $700,000 to the Congressional Leadership Fund, a pair of super PACs aligned with Republican congressional leaders.

Dick DeVos donated $500,000 to the AFC Victory Fund, a national super PAC prioritizing education freedom and backing pro-school choice candidates.

The media department for the Orlando Magic did not respond to a request for comment or a confirmation.

Other notable contributions from NBA owners include: Atlanta Hawks owner Tony Ressler’s $2 million donation to the Americans for Prosperity Action PAC, Sacramento Kings owner Vivek Ranadivé’s $250,000 donation to the RNC and the over $160,000 in bipartisan spending from Miami Heat owner Micky Arison.

Fertitta, the ambassador and Houston Rockets owner, gave $200,000 to the Republican National Committee this election.

Landry’s Inc., Fertitta’s dining, hospitality, entertainment and gaming company, referred The Sun to the company’s PR department, which did not respond to a request for comment and confirmation.

The Sun analyzed FEC records from Jan. 1, 2025, through Oct. 14, 2026, to gauge spending among sports owners from the NBA, NFL, MLB and NHL. (Many NBA owners also own a WNBA team.)

Individual donors may donate unlimited amounts of money to super PACs, which in turn may spend unlimited amounts to advocate for or against political candidates. But individuals may only donate $3,500 to individual candidates’ campaigns once per election. Donations to national party committees such as the Republican National Committee and Democratic National Committee are also limited by law, but not as much.

Tepid Spending Among Washington Team Owners

In the nation’s capital city, Washington team owners were relatively constrained in their political spending this election cycle.

Washington Commanders owner Josh Harris gave $250,000 to the Senate Leadership Fund, a Republican super PAC. He also donated $5,000 to the NFL’s Gridiron PAC, to which the majority of league’s owners contribute. Minority team owners Mark Ein, and Mark Lipschultz matched Harris’s donation.
Josh.Harris.1 (8256x5504, AR: 1.50)A spokesman for Harris didn’t respond to a request for comment.

The NFL and MLB are the two major sports leagues that sponsor a federal PAC.

Monumental Sports CEO Ted Leonsis, who owns Washington’s Capitals, Wizards, Mystics and basketball G League’s Go-Go, gave $7,000 across the primary and general elections to both Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Maryland) and Sen. Mark Warner (D-Virginia). Leonsis gave an additional $10,000 to a PAC for Warner.

Leonsis is also listed as the donor of a $105,000 contribution to the Monumental Sports PAC, but that’s actually a corporate contribution, a source with knowledge of his donations told The Sun.

Leonsis is credited for the amount as Monumental Sports controlling owner. He further gave $3,000 to the Democratic Party of Virginia, donating $20,000 total outside of his company’s PAC. Leonsis is a longtime donor to the Democratic Party.

Nationals owner Mark Lerner gave $5,000 to MLB’s Commissioner PAC, and gave another $7,500 to Dylan Hewitt (D), a candidate for a House seat in New York’s 21st Congressional District. Lerner also donated $1,200 to Cait Conley (D), another congressional candidate running in New York’s 17th District.

The lack of political spending extends north up Interstate 95. Both Baltimore sports owners — baseball’s David Rubenstein (Orioles) and football’s Stephen Bisciotti (Ravens) — each gave $5,000 to their respective league PACs.

Blame Canada?

The National Hockey League is the least politically active professional sports league, perhaps because the league has seven Canadian teams with Canadian owners and foreign donations are prohibited in U.S. elections.

Philip Anschutz, owner of the Los Angeles Kings, was the NHL’s biggest spender giving $2.34 million this midterm cycle, spread among dozens of Republican candidates and committees.
Philip.A (5266x3511, AR: 1.50)That includes $620,200 to the National Republican Congressional Committee, $509,100 to the Johnson Leadership Fund and $75,000 to the Scalise Leadership Fund.

Tampa Bay Lightning owner Marc Lipschultz followed, giving Republicans a $445,100 boost.

Former Pro Athletes Attract Owner Cash

A pro football showdown is brewing in Arizona, but it doesn’t involve a stadium.

Jay Feely, a former placekicker who played in the NFL for more than a decade, is running to replace fellow Republican Rep. David Schweikert, who did not run for reelection and instead ran for Arizona governor. (He lost in a primary.)

Feely’s journeyman career — he played for six teams, including the Arizona Cardinals — is seemingly paying dividends, with NFL owners from six teams (four of which Feely played for) collectively putting over $36,000 toward his campaign.
Jay.Feely (5184x3456, AR: 1.50)Cardinals owner Michael Bidwill donated $7,000 directly to Feely’s campaign earlier this year, split between his primary and general election campaigns, according to The Sun’s review of campaign finance records.

Feely has also received support from the sports world outside of the NFL’s franchise owners: NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell and former NBA star Charles Barkley, the latter of whom resides in Arizona, both donated $7,000 to the ex-kicker’s campaign, the maximum allowable under federal law between primary and general elections. Minnesota Vikings coach Kevin O’Connell also gave $500, according to FEC data. O’Connell and Feely played together on the Jets in 2009.

Feely’s opponent, Democrat Amish Shah, also has an NFL connection: Shah previously worked as a team doctor for the New York Jets. This included Feely’s tenure with the Jets during the 2008 and 2009 seasons. No NFL team owners, who largely lean Republican in their partisan donations, have financially backed Shah since Jan. 1, 2025, according to The Sun’s analysis.

Texas Rangers owner Ray Davis put $7,500 behind a joint fundraising committee tied to former MLB all-star Mark Teixeira, who began his 14-season major league career with the franchise and is now running to represent Texas’ 21st Congressional District, which stretches from San Antonio north toward Austin and west through largely rural south-central Texas counties.

Teixeira has been a fundraising magnet for Republicans. House Republicans are bringing the Republican far outside his district, Politico reported, joining House Speaker Mike Johnson throughout New York state — Teixeira played for the New York Yankees during much of his career.
Mark.Texeira (2671x2152, AR: 1.24)Much of Teixeira’s campaign is self-financed: The Republican loaned it just under $2.8 million throughout late 2025 and early 2026, according to campaign finance reports. Teixeira earned over $222.1 million over his MLB career, according to Spotrac.

Democrat Colin Allred, the former House member and linebacker with the Tennessee Titans who is running in Texas’ 33rd Congressional District, which includes parts of Dallas and surrounding suburbs, hasn’t gotten the same treatment from his old employer.

Instead, Allred has largely funded his House campaign through a combination of small-dollar donors and leftover funds from his failed Senate campaign, according to FEC data. Allred dropped out before the Texas Senate primary and endorsed Rep. Jasmine Crockett, who ultimately fell in a primary to Democratic nominee James Talarico.

Neither Feely, Shah, Teixeira nor Allred responded to The Sun’s request for comment.

Amy Adams Strunk, controlling owner of the Tennessee franchise, where Allred played, has only made one federal donation this cycle: $5,000 to Gridiron-PAC this past March, according to FEC data.

entries.title: The DOJ’s Unlikely Point Man
entries.summary: Stanley Woodward Jr. said he never saw himself working at the Justice Department, but he’s now stepping in when Trump’s priorities are in court.
entries.content:
Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward Jr., once a defense lawyer connected to President Donald Trump’s inner circle, has become the Justice Department’s go-to for the most politically sensitive court cases.

He's a fixer, of sorts, but his appearance on the docket or a legal filing often signals a more contentious turn. The cases are high profile, close to Trump's interests and frequently at moments when judges are thwarting the president’s will.

Katie Phang, a journalist who sued the government over the administration’s rollout of files related to notorious sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, said she came up with a nickname for the annoyance she experienced when he showed up in her case.

“I call Woodward ‘the seagull.’ You know when you're at the beach and one swoops in and steals your french fries?” she said.

Woodward, the DOJ’s No. 3 ranking official, a position which has historically been managerial only, appeared on a filing in her high-profile case after the government did not comply with a court-ordered deadline to produce documents, including records that mention allegations against Trump.

He also swooped in to preemptively challenge the results of the Senate race in Alaska, a move that was criticized as a Trump administration attempt at affecting the outcome of the election there. He has defended the president’s vision of a giant White House ballroom and tangled with the judge blocking work at the D.C. golf course Trump wants to overhaul.

The political appointee was the sole DOJ signer on the settlement agreement in Trump’s lawsuit against the IRS that set up a $1.8 billion fund “anti-weaponization fund” — an agreement a judge later concluded was the result of Trump and the Justice Department manipulating the judicial process for the “imprimatur of legality for an unlawful settlement.” 

Last week, Woodward dropped into three separate cases to demand that judges be disqualified from matters connected to Trump priorities, part of the Trump administration’s pushback against judges they say have treated the government unfairly.

In Minnesota, Woodward signed a judicial misconduct complaint in September against two federal judges over comments they made to The New York Times related to the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown in the state.

Last week, he signed motions to kick those judges off of two immigration cases, accusing the judges of “improper political commentary” that he said raised doubts about their ability to fairly adjudicate the cases.

And in D.C., he has stepped into a challenge to Trump’s plans to renovate and expand a golf course at East Potomac Park. He’s seeking to disqualify Judge Ana Reyes, who has blocked work on the project and held a tense three-hour hearing in which she harshly criticized the government for having deceived her with its actions related to tree removal over a recent holiday weekend.

In a motion, Woodward called her behavior “nothing short of egregious” and “histrionics.”

It’s a case Trump has inserted himself into as well, with social media posts that describe the plans, criticize Reyes and declare that the course will be closed to start the project Nov. 15 regardless of the courts. “The judge has absolutely no right to hold up this very important and beautiful Project,” Trump posted.

Woodward had told Reyes at an Oct. 19 hearing that there was no plan to close the course on Nov. 15 — and then in a Wednesday filing, he said plans to close it that day are now underway.

Woodward is currently listed as a lawyer in at least 19 cases filed since Trump returned to power, according to court records, more involvement in ground-level litigation than typical for the nation’s associate attorney general, a role that has traditionally overseen all U.S. government civil litigation.

“It is, in my experience, unprecedented,” said Bill Baer, who had that job as acting associate AG for nearly a year during the Obama administration and had previously spent years reporting to that office.

Previous associate attorneys general have held weekly meetings with the divisions that handle civil rights, antitrust and environmental cases to develop strategies for defending the presidential administration’s most important issues.

During the previous administration, the job meant figuring out how to shape the defense of President Joe Biden’s student loan program and face off against corporate superpowers such as Apple and Ticketmaster. But under this administration, Woodward has added another task to his portfolio: appearing in court to personally press Trump’s will.

During a podcast in May with America First Legal, the conservative outfit started by White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, Woodward said that “what gets me up in the morning is knowing President Trump understands very clearly why the Justice Department is and was in need of reform. He has tasked me with the awesome responsibility of helping us get there.”

And he noted the outsized importance of the DOJ — and his responsibilities overseeing its civil litigation — fighting over the legality of Trump’s executive orders in an attempt to secure court rulings that will hamstring the next president from simply revoking them with the stroke of a pen.

“The president keenly understands that his legacy will be shaped by the outcome of the litigation that is happening in the courts over the executive actions that he is taking,” Woodward said.

Baer called it “shocking” that an associate attorney general would insert themselves in ongoing litigation rather than direct it from afar with general strategic advice, saying that Woodward’s personal involvement hints at the administration’s difficulty in getting career prosecutors to put their names on filings.

“That’s a signal right there that career people who understand their ethical obligations to the public, their ethical obligations to the bar, are not willing to put all that at risk to support a brief that is lacking in legal merit,” he told The Washington Sun.

DOJ spokesperson Katie Kenlein, addressing questions about why an official of his rank has inserted himself into so many cases, said the department “can’t speak to why previous [associate attorneys general] were not involved.”

“Are you critiquing Stanley wanting to do his job/suggesting DOJ would be better off with someone who wasn’t so ‘involved?’ I’ll point you to his quote which still stands,” she wrote in an email.

Kenlein directed The Sun to a 2022 Politico story where Woodward was quoted as saying, “I’ll sleep when I’m dead.” That story also described Woodward as a legal nerd and “neither a bomb-thrower nor a headline-seeker.”

Woodward said in the May podcast he had “virtually no agenda” coming into the Justice Department, and pointed to his experience with the tactics of Biden-era prosecutors as something that led him to his current role.

"I frankly never saw myself working in the Department of Justice, because everything that the department stood for, especially in the last four years, was antithetical to what I believed,” he said.

Long before Woodward became a Trumpworld insider, he graduated from Catholic University of America’s law school and later returned to teach pretrial litigation and lead its alumni council. He became licensed to practice law in Washington in 2010 and eight years later earned recognition from the D.C. Bar — the same one he’d later attack — by becoming its pro bono attorney of the year for representing poor tenants who faced eviction. His growing local reputation got him recommended by the local Judicial Nominating Commission for a spot on the D.C. Superior Court bench in 2020.

His eventual dive into the legal circles of MAGA began in the months after the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol building. Woodward represented several rioters, including the wife of an Oath Keeper and a former Trump State Department employee. In the summer of 2022, he started defending Peter Navarro, a former Trump White House official who had boasted about a failed plan to keep Trump in power dubbed “Green Bay Sweep” — and was convicted of contempt of Congress after refusing to testify about it before the House Jan. 6 Committee.

Earning the trust of the MAGA cause, he was tapped to represent Walt Nauta, Trump’s valet who was accused of helping Trump try to hide boxes of records when federal investigators were looking into classified documents located at his private Mar-a-Lago estate.

One moment in August 2022 came to define Woodward’s alignment with MAGA — and cemented his relationship with Trump, according to a source familiar with the situation. Woodward, as the attorney for Nauta, met with prosecutors who’d eventually become part of Special Counsel Jack Smith’s team.

In Woodword’s version of the story, the prosecutors expressed a desire to obtain Nauta’s cooperation against Trump, but one of them said he didn’t take Woodward to be a “Trump attorney” — and casually mentioned how Woodward was up for a judicial nomination.

Defense lawyers reported it to a D.C. federal judge as a veiled threat of political retribution. Trump’s defense lawyer circle used the incident in the Mar-a-Lago case as evidence of vindictive prosecution — and sources cited it to The Washington Sun in late 2024 as a key element in the incoming Trump administration’s quest for retribution.

“It showed his loyalty,” said a source familiar with the episode.

Woodward said on the podcast that Trump was prosecuted under a novel theory that had never been tested, and 300 Jan. 6 participants were prosecuted under a theory that the Supreme Court two years later concluded was wrong.

“I feel like we were aggressively prosecuting on novel theories, and that just makes my blood boil,” Woodward said. “But the president asked me to come, and as you all know, when the president asks, you don't say no. Although I did twice, and the third time, it was clear what the ultimatum was, and so here we are."

He spent the first months of the new administration as a White House lawyer before getting Trump’s nomination to be the No. 3 at the DOJ.

Woodward digitally signed a Justice Department motion back in April defending Trump’s planned White House ballroom that was widely noticed for a style more closely resembling a Trump Truth Social post than a legal filing.

“‘The National Trust for Historic Preservation’ is a beautiful name,” it said. “But even their name is FAKE because when they add the words ‘in the United States’ to the National Trust for Historic Preservation, it makes it sound like a Governmental Agency, which it is not.”

It mocked the trust, saying “they suffer from Trump Derangement Syndrome.” And the use of all caps continued later: “Congress has never dictated or tampered with the zoning, permitting, or architectural aspects of any Project, especially one being given FREE OF CHARGE AS A GIFT TO THE COUNTRY!”

Kenlein, the DOJ spokesperson, did not answer a question about whether Woodward had written the legal briefs on his own or was taking dictation from Trump. However, she defended his recent filings taking on district court judges.

“Judges are routinely persecuting lawyers who take positions contrary to their views. Woodward has consistently been willing to stand up on behalf of line prosecutors who represent the American people,” she said in an email.

Woodward has a tendency to show up when a case reaches an inflection point, according to several people involved in those cases, who say he appears either when the understaffed and overwhelmed DOJ mishandles a case or when a politically sensitive issue is at stake.

“He shows up like a bad penny,” Phang said.

In Phang’s Epstein-related case, Woodward formally appeared the day after U.S. District Judge Emmet Sullivan ordered the DOJ to comply with Congress’ new law and produce documents, such as FBI agents’ handwritten interview notes, foreign-language materials and records that mention allegations against Trump.

The DOJ hadn’t bothered to file an answer in court — blowing the initial deadline by 90 days and submitting one only after Phang’s lawyers asked the judge to compel the government to do so. When the government finally did, the document bore the names of Woodward and Andrew Block, a senior counsel at the associate attorney general’s office.

And it came with Trumpian flair, calling Trump “the leader of the most transparent Presidential Administration in the history of this great Nation,” and describing DOJ’s effort to release the Epstein files as a “Herculean task.”

Woodward swooped into a Massachusetts fight over offshore wind turbines in January, just four days before arguments over whether Vineyard Wind could challenge the Trump administration’s decision to block — on national security grounds — a $4.5 billion project that was 95% complete and had been producing power for over a year.

Trump has long been an enemy of tall turbines and renewable energy, and the halt came from his executive order targeting the industry. Woodward appeared for a scheduling conference ahead of the arguments, and his name was on a recent status update indicating that the national security “review remains ongoing.” That same month, he appeared in another lawsuit over a halted wind energy project in New York.

In September, Woodward entered the fray in an ongoing lawsuit over the Trump administration’s new dietary guidelines. Mark Kennedy, an attorney with the Physicians Committee for Responsible Medicine, said in an interview that the new guidelines are “central to this new MAHA concept” — and that a government loss in court would be a huge setback for the White House.

“This would throw all that away,” Kennedy said.

And Woodward signed the DOJ’s lawsuit in May attempting to block the D.C. Court of Appeals from disciplining Jeffrey Clark, a high-ranking DOJ official in the first Trump administration who played a role in the president’s attempts to overturn the 2020 election by drafting a proposal to have the DOJ issue a letter to swing states citing supposed irregularities to pressure them to appoint alternative electors.

The knives came out last week, when MAGA influencer Laura Loomer accused Woodward of mishandling a case involving government settlements for U.S. military service members who claim they were exposed to contaminated drinking water at Marine Corps Base Camp Lejeune. She called him a “Democrat Associate Attorney General who is low balling sick US Marines who have been diagnosed with cancer.”

Several Trump-aligned conservatives rose to Woodward’s defense. Blanche himself posted a reply, calling Woodward “one of DOJ’s best fighters” and a “patriot who is fighting for POTUS and the American people every day.”

The attorney general also noted who at DOJ makes the decisions about Camp Lejeune settlements, “consulting with and keeping the White House counsel’s office.” Later that night, Trump himself weighed in on the litigation strategy at a campaign rally in North Carolina — and tied it directly to politics.

"If we win the House and the Senate, I am directing the Department of Justice to settle all remaining legitimate claims as soon as possible, and get it off the books and get it finished,” the president said. “So if we don't win, there's no money. If we do win, you’re getting it."

On Tuesday, DOJ said it “had approved 3,780 more settlements for $860 million more than the previous administration. We are in lock step with the White House and Department of War on protecting our veterans.”

One former top DOJ official, speaking to The Washington Sun, expressed incredulity that Woodward could have time for run-of-the-mill lawyering. The cracks might be starting to show.

In the Alaska lawsuit, a federal judge is fast-tracking the case and has already expressed skepticism over the timing of the suit, which came “after Alaskans had already begun casting their ballots.”

On Tuesday, a state lawyer representing Alaska in the case, racing to meet the court’s deadline, noted that the listed DOJ attorney in the case had referred her to Woodward.

“When I called Mr. Woodward, I got his voicemail and left a message,” attorney Margaret Paton Walsh wrote. “I have not heard back from him at the time of filing.”

entries.title: Major D.C. Landlord Sued Over Excessive Fees for Tenants
entries.summary: A D.C. renter claims Vivmark Residential charged him and others thousands of dollars in fees the D.C. Council has ruled illegal.
entries.content:
When Sam Mather’s landlord changed his locks to digital “smart home” ones, they went a bridge too far by charging him for the pleasure, according to a new class action lawsuit filed Thursday.

The lawsuit alleges that Vivmark Residential, a major national landlord, has been charging tenants across the 5,300 units it owns and manages in D.C. fees for having keyless doors, digital thermostats, trash removal, access to hot water from a central boiler and third-party billing.

All told, the fees — which the lawsuit argues are excessive “junk” fees that the D.C. Council and attorney general have specifically ruled illegal — cost Mather, the plaintiff in the case, more than $2,000 in the five years he lived at 2501 Porter St. NW, one of dozens of apartment buildings the company owns and manages across the D.C. metro area, the lawsuit says.

The suit attacks a “proliferating problem” in D.C. housing that burdens renters already struggling to navigate a costly rental market, Tara Mikkilineni, a lead attorney in the case, told The Washington Sun.

“It's already so hard to find affordable housing [in D.C.], and on top of that, you're being charged for these basic services the landlord is required to provide. It really eats away at folks' disposable income,” Mikkilineni said.

A spokesperson for Vivmark Residential, a company formed in August by the merger of AvalonBay Communities and Equity Residential with headquarters in Chicago and Arlington, did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the lawsuit or why the fees were charged.

“For corporate landlords, there's a lot of appeal in packing on these fees that create additional consistent revenue streams,” Mikkilineni said.

Tacking on fees could be attractive to property management firms in D.C. operating on slim profit margins and dealing with high rent delinquencies. That reality is why there are fewer reputable property management companies than ever in the District to contract with, landlords say.

“Property managers are often paid as a percentage of rental income collected. When collections fall, that fee may no longer support the time and effort needed to manage a property facing significant operating and maintenance challenges,” said Dean Hunter, the CEO of D.C.’s Small Multifamily Owners Association.

But companies aren’t allowed to charge their way into solvency. D.C. renters are protected by law from “junk fees” — which the D.C. attorney general’s office defines as “a blanket term for any fees that are unclear, are not used for their stated purpose, or are used to cover a service a landlord is required to provide to rent a livable space.”

That includes charges for services the landlord should be providing anyway when renting out a livable space, the AG’s guidance on the issue says, like service fees for providing utilities.

The D.C. Council clarified earlier this year that housing providers are barred from charging tenants for “services that they are required to provide under the implied warranty of habitability” and that should be covered by rent, specifically naming lockable doors and trash removal as examples.

The lawsuit — filed in D.C. Superior Court by law firms Halperin Petersen & Mikkilineni LLP, Tycko & Zavareei LLP and Migliaccio & Rathod LLP — seeks a jury trial, damages and disgorgement of ill-gotten gains.

entries.title: Trump Talks to Grok. Democrats Plan to Find Out What He’s Saying.
entries.summary: The president and his staff have been asked to archive prompts submitted to several popular chatbots, an indication that Democrats may seek to reveal those documents.
entries.content:
Congressional Democrats are pushing to access records related to President Donald Trump and other White House staffers’ interactions with AI chatbots, and they demanded on Wednesday that members of the administration preserve their online records.

Democrats don’t currently have subpoena power to compel the government to release the records, but the request is an indication that the line of inquiry will be a priority for Democratic members of the House Oversight and Judiciary Committees should the party retake control of the chamber following next week’s midterm elections.

In a letter sent to the president by Reps. Jamie Raskin and Robert Garcia Wednesday, the congressmen — the top Democrats on Judiciary and Oversight, respectively — asked the president if the executive branch has been soliciting advice from Grok, the AI chatbot created by Elon Musk’s social media company X, to carry out official responsibilities.

“If the American President is relying on the policy advice of a Musk-designed, Hitler-friendly chatbot with a predilection for child pornography in order to carry out his official duties, Americans have a right to know,” the lawmakers wrote, referring to recent reports that claim Trump has been using the notoriously mercurial technology.

They added that their ultimate goal is to find out whether the Trump administration is leaking national security information to AI chatbots and determine what role AI may have in forming federal policy.

The congressmen are requesting that Trump, his staff and advisers archive prompts submitted to Grok, ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Perplexity and the AI-generated responses to those prompts for posterity.

The lawmakers raised concerns about national security risks that could stem from AI chatbots being used throughout the federal government.

“Preserving the President’s and his advisors’ AI prompts is thus essential to preserving an accurate historical record and informing future administrations against the gaping national security vulnerabilities created by this Administration’s apparent reliance on unsecured, privately operated AI systems,” they wrote.

In a statement to The Washington Sun, the White House said it preserves all required records in accordance with the law.

Earlier this month, TechCrunch reported that Trump told Musk last year that he was spending hours talking to Grok.

According to the outlet, the president sought the chatbot’s advice on carrying out the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro.

Grok apparently encouraged Trump to carry out the attack, stating Maduro is a “deeply unpopular dictator and that many Venezuelans would likely celebrate his downfall,” TechCrunch reported.

Trump later ordered Maduro’s capture without congressional approval.

Following the military action, Trump thought Grok was “ingenious,” according to the technology publication.

The lawmakers are concerned the president “consulted Grok—but not Congress—on your military deployment to Venezuela, circumventing Congress’s constitutional power to declare war.”

The lawmakers pointed to the U.S. military’s strike on an Iranian elementary school that killed at least 123 children as an example of what could happen as a result of errors perpetuated by AI. The strike stemmed from the military’s “overreliance on artificial-intelligence technology,” the letter says.

In another instance earlier this year, the U.S. military nearly intercepted a Chinese vessel in the Middle East that was suspected of transporting components for a nuclear weapons program. The claim stemmed from a report, but military officials later determined the author of the report used an AI chatbot that misidentified the ship’s cargo.

“This was not an isolated or aberrational mistake,” the Democrats say in the letter.

The congressmen assert the executive branch’s AI chats must be preserved under the 1978 Presidential Records Act.

The law establishes public ownership of records created by presidents and their staff. The National Archives and Records Administration stores and preserves presidential and vice presidential records generated in the course of their official duties.

The lawmakers argue that AI prompts submitted by staff fall within the definition of presidential records, and they are separately requesting a closed-door briefing regarding the executive branch’s use of AI by Nov. 11.

Earlier this year, the National Archives and Records Administration released guidance on AI use for federal agencies and legal counsel.

The guidance states that agencies’ use of AI platforms does not, in and of itself, result in the creation of federal records — although there are several instances in which “subsequent use of AI-generated materials in agency business may result in the creation of federal records.”

Jason R. Baron, the former director of litigation at the National Archives and Records Administration, said the federal government is in uncharted territory when it comes to preserving AI records.

"If staffers are drafting prompts on a Gen AI platform and then using the responses in the course of government business, then they may well be considered presidential records or federal records,” he said.

But just because a staffer uses AI doesn’t mean all communications are considered presidential or federal records. Chatbots should not be used for sensitive or classified information, Baron said.

"I can also conceive of there being prompts that one asks that remain personal to the person who's asking them,” he added.

entries.title: Ken Paxton Sticks With the Voters He Knows
entries.summary: The Texas Senate candidate is focused on turning out base voters rather than building a broader coalition.
entries.content:
EDINBURG, Texas — Ken Paxton, Texas’ attorney general and its Republican Senate nominee, is homing in on the ultraconservative voters who have long powered his political career in his final push to win the grueling race.

Paxton has largely leaned into familiar conservative messages — like attacking transgender people and aligning himself with President Donald Trump — betting that the Republican base will be enough to carry him to victory in November. The approach reflects a political calculation that has long worked for Republicans in Texas, which is to energize conservative voters and capitalize on the state's conservative bent.

It’s a risky strategy for a general election that presupposes Texas is not the battleground just about everyone else — including some Republicans — think it is.

"Politics is about addition, not subtraction. Winners broaden their appeal. Losers run primaries in generals," said a Republican strategist familiar with Texas politics, speaking on the condition of anonymity to offer a candid assessment of the race. They argued that Paxton's approach could prove costly.

"When Ken loses, this will be a big reason why."

Paxton has been a longtime ally of Trump, whose endorsement of him over Sen. John Cornyn in the Republican primary helped propel him to victory. Trump carried Texas by nearly 14 percentage points in 2024, a data point that shows the considerable advantage Republicans have enjoyed in statewide elections.

In the months since Paxton won the primary, though, it’s become an expensive race that both parties see as a priority. In a state that hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate in decades, polls show an unexpectedly competitive race between Paxton and his opponent, Democratic state Rep. James Talarico.

“Paxton's only conceivable path to victory is to get Republicans to rally around the Trump standard and run up the score. Paxton is hoping that party loyalty will overcome voters' reservations about him,” said Dennis Lennox, a Republican strategist based in Michigan. “The bigger question for Republicans: How many Senate races around the country will they lose because hundreds of millions of dollars were spent to save Paxton in Texas?”

Paxton's campaign has continued to emphasize his conservative credentials while attacking Talarico over his positions on culture war issues. His ads have sought to portray Talarico as too liberal for Texas.

“He wants to transition our kids. He wants to transition Texas off of oil and gas. How about we transition him and his crazy ideas right out of Texas?” Paxton said recently at a rally in Edinburg, Texas.

Talarico’s campaign did not respond to a request for comment.

Talarico is presenting himself as a candidate willing to engage with Texans who disagree with him and leaning heavily on his Christian faith, seeking to challenge the Republican Party's long-standing advantage among religious voters.

Paxton has also sought to mobilize religious conservatives in an effort to win the seat, including through a group called Pastors for Paxton that recently announced endorsements from dozens of Houston-area pastors, underscoring his appeal to Texas Evangelical voters.

“Talarico believes that God is nonbinary,” Paxton has said on the stump. “If someone can show me where that is in the scriptures, I'd love to see it.”

The Paxton campaign did not respond to a request for comment on this story.

Paxton presents his own unique challenges as a candidate, given that his political career has been marked by controversy and he needs to win over voters who have reservations about him.

In 2023, he was impeached by the Republican-controlled Texas House on more than a dozen articles, including bribery and unfitness for office, but was acquitted by the state Senate in a high-profile trial. Since then, he’s faced a messy public divorce from state Sen. Angela Paxton, though she has urged voters to cast their ballots for the Republican ticket (without naming Paxton).

Earlier this year, Cornyn summarized what it could mean to have Paxton at the top of the ticket as “dead weight.” He has not campaigned for Paxton in the general and has become outspoken about some Trump administration goals as his retirement nears.

“I refuse to allow a flawed, self-centered and shameless candidate like Ken Paxton to risk everything we’ve worked so hard to build over these many years,” Cornyn said when the polls for the Senate primary closed in March. “There is simply too much at stake in this midterm election for our state and for our country.”

entries.title: DOJ Announces Indictments of Kenyans in Student Loan Fraud
entries.summary: Prosecutors say the defendants used the identities of Americans to enroll as “ghost students” to pocket student aid payments.
entries.content:
The DOJ announced the first five indictments in an investigation into a large-scale student loan fraud scheme.

Colin McDonald, the assistant attorney general for DOJ’s National Fraud Enforcement Division, said the agency identified five Kenyan nationals who conspired to use Americans’ identities to enroll in colleges as “ghost students” to pocket student aid payments.

“The methods used in these schemes are increasingly sophisticated. Some use super intelligence to fill out college applications and complete coursework, so it looks like the ghost student is actually completing the class,” McDonald said at a news conference. “The goal is to keep the ghost student in school for as long as possible, semester after semester after semester, stealing money from the taxpayer.”

The investigation, referred to as Operation Ghostbusters, includes the Justice Department, U.S. attorneys' offices, the FBI, the Department of Education, U.S. Customs and Border Protection and the State Department.

In Nebraska, a grand jury indicted Francis Mogambi earlier this month on charges of theft of government money and aggravated identity theft. Prosecutors say Mogambi worked with associates in Kenya to steal U.S. identities and enroll individuals in college without their knowledge, then redirected federal aid payments to himself and co-conspirators in Kenya.

Last week, Mabed Utate-Alberto, George Alfau Mendez and Patricia Perez were arrested on charges of conspiracy to commit wire fraud. The group is accused of siphoning over $1.5 million in student loans funds into Kenyan bank accounts.

And in Virginia, a grand jury indicted another Kenyan national last week with conspiracy to commit wire fraud and student aid fraud, the Justice Department said. The defendant in the still sealed case conspired to use the stolen identities of U.S. citizens to submit false federal student aid applications, resulting in over 700 fraudulently obtained federal student aid refund deposits and over $1.4 million stolen in student aid, prosecutors said.

The department seized over $750,000 from a cryptocurrency account tied to the scheme and laundered through a larger network, the DOJ said. McDonald said the scheme has likely been going on since at least 2021 and has resulted in “several hundred million dollars lost.”

Nicholas Kent, the under secretary of education, attributed the increase in student loan fraud to the Biden administration, who he said “turned off nearly every fraud detection measure.” He said the Education Department has created new tools in federal financial aid applications that require students to show an ID, an effort that has resulted in nearly $600 million in savings in six months and prevented more than $2 billion in attempted federal student aid fraud, Kent said at a press conference.

“Let me be very clear: every dollar that falls into the hands of a fraudster is $1 that will not only go to a fraudster, but not go to a poor or low-income student,” Kent said at the news conference. “We will not stand by as fraudsters rob opportunities from our students to learn, grow, and to thrive, and we will not allow international actors to pocket the money American taxpayers have entrusted us with.”

Lower-resource institutions, such as community colleges that have lower tuition and fees, are usually the target of fraud, Kent and McDonald said. Americans who have never been to college are also targets because their lack of a previous student aid application avoids alerting Education Department systems.

Heith Janke, assistant director of the FBI’s Criminal Division, said the agency has opened 45 investigations across dozens of offices involving “ghost students.” The agency identified over 830,000 potentially fraudulent student aid accounts created by using the personally identifiable information of U.S. citizens, he said.

“What is even more horrifying is that our victims did not even know their information and their PII was being used,” Janke said. “You could go completely unaware until that loan repayment notification came in, which could be years down the road.”

entries.title: Spirit Midfielder Hal Hershfelt Is Out for the Season With a Torn ACL
entries.summary: Hershfelt has been one of the Spirit’s most reliable players this season, leaving the team without a key contributor ahead of the NWSL playoffs.
entries.content:
The Spirit will have to play their regular-season finale and the playoffs without one of their most reliable players.

The team announced Thursday that midfielder Hal Hershfelt will miss the rest of the season after tearing her right ACL in Sunday’s 2-1 loss to the Kansas City Current. The 25-year-old was injured in the match’s 16th minute when she was trying to stop a cross by Croix Bethune that set up the game-winning goal. Hershfelt played four more minutes before being subbed out.

ACL recoveries tend to take more than six months, which means Hershfelt could miss a significant portion of the 2027 season, too.

In 2026, Hershfelt appeared in 31 matches with a goal and an assist, both of which were game-winners. She also scored a game-winner against Seattle in the 81st minute in May and assisted on Trinity Rodman’s goal against Chicago in September. She has been a defensive force in the Spirit’s midfield as well, known for disrupting opposing attacks.

The Spirit selected Hershfelt fifth overall out of Clemson in the 2024 NWSL draft, and for the past three seasons she has been a reliable presence in the midfield while occasionally battling injuries. She missed seven matches in 2025 with an ankle sprain and played through a leg injury in the championship match against Gotham FC.

The Spirit are third in the league standings entering Sunday’s matchup against Chicago and have already clinched a playoff spot. The team could finish as high as second or as low as fifth, depending on the results of the regular season’s final games.
