entries.title: Senate Democrats Demand Answers on Plans to Use Public Land Use for Data Centers
entries.summary: The effort comes after The Washington Sun reported the Trump administration is considering applications for several data centers on public lands.
entries.content:
Senate Democrats are asking Interior Secretary Doug Burgum to cease efforts to build data centers on public lands in light of The Washington Sun’s reporting that revealed the extent of the development the Trump administration is considering.

Sens. Ron Wyden (Oregon), Jeff Merkley (Oregon) and Alex Padilla (California) wrote in a letter to Burgum that the “complete lack of transparency” over his meetings with data center developers and investors over the past year and a half is compounding their concerns. The senators asked the Interior Department to provide information about Burgum’s role in the agency’s handling of public lands.

The Sun reported that the Trump administration was considering proposals for at least a dozen data center projects on federal public lands across six Western states — Arizona, Idaho, Nevada, Oregon, Utah and Wyoming.

According to The Sun’s review of Burgum’s calendar, the Secretary met with dozens of technology and energy executives last year. Those meetings included a conversation with Amazon CEO Andy Jassy about permitting, infrastructure and technology “to support data center growth.”

The senators also wrote that they had concerns over “numerous risks posed to communities” by data centers, including water use that could exacerbate drought conditions in the West.

“Effectively privatizing public lands owned by American taxpayers sends a clear message that the Trump administration continues to prioritize the profits of tech CEOs and shareholders over the American people that rely on public lands for hunting, fishing, recreation, and livestock grazing,” they wrote.

The Center for Western Priorities has identified 17 applications to build data centers on federal public lands, along with 13 “likely” applications for infrastructure that could support those developments.

No data centers are currently located on federal public lands. Kate Groetzinger, communications manager at the Center for Western Priorities, has surfaced concerns that the Bureau of Land Management has not established a legal basis for allowing data centers on public lands, as they have done with technologies like wind and solar. Instead, BLM would have to rely on a provision that allows for facilities that are “necessary” and “in the public interests” to be on public lands.

“Whether AI data centers serve the ‘public interest’ is an open question—but poll after poll suggests that Americans think they do not,” she wrote.

The Interior Department declined to comment, saying they “do not comment on congressional correspondence through the media.”

entries.title: Alaska Governor Doesn’t Commit to Certifying Senate Race if Peltola Wins
entries.summary: The state is currently involved in litigation with the federal government over two Dan Sullivans appearing on the ballot.
entries.content:
Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy sidestepped questions about whether he planned to certify the state’s Senate race if Democrat Mary Peltola wins, telling NewsNation on Thursday that his office won’t send a “scam” to Washington.

“We're going to follow the law, and if we conclude that there was this, uh, mis — there were things that should not have happened, let me put it that way, that are illegal, we will act on that. And that may, in fact, impact whether somebody is seated in this U.S. Senate,” Dunleavy told NewsNation on Thursday.

The governor announced Thursday that he was opening a probe into Democrats’ alleged “scheme,” in which Peltola campaign staffers and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee had conspired to recruit people named Dan Sullivan to run against incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) as spoiler candidates.

Dan J. Sullivan, who will appear on the ballot in November, Peltola’s campaign and other Democrats have denied the allegations as reported in The New York Times this week.

The article has bolstered Republican efforts to derail Peltola’s Senate bid.

The Alaska Supreme Court ruled this spring that the second Dan Sullivan would remain on the ballot — a decision that is now central to President Donald Trump’s decision to have the Justice Department sue Alaska in hopes of blocking certification of the race if the incumbent Sullivan loses.

When NewsNation pressed Dunleavy on not answering “yes” to a question about certifying the election’s results, the governor said residents want him to ensure they don’t send a “scam” to Washington.

“We started our investigation here a day ago — we never, again, we did not want this individual on our ballot,” Dunleavy said, referring to candidate Dan J. Sullivan. “It was the Supreme Court of Alaska that made that decision, unfortunately.”

He added that if state Supreme Court justices had known that information earlier, “they probably would have arrived at a different conclusion.”

The Justice Department on Thursday issued several subpoenas in its criminal investigation into whether Peltola’s campaign was involved in recruiting Dan J. Sullivan as part of an alleged effort to confuse voters in the hotly contested race.

Also on Thursday, the Trump administration filed an amended complaint and asked the court to block a previous motion to dismiss the case filed by Peltola’s campaign and the DSCC. Government lawyers argue that new allegations in the Times story provide more details about the “conspiracy by the Peltola Campaign and the DSCC to mislead voters.”
entries.author: Gavin J. Quinton

entries.title: Ramaswamy Pulls Controversial Ad Featuring His Opponent’s Estranged Mother
entries.summary: The Republican gubernatorial candidate said the campaign ad “ran to completion.”
entries.content:
Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy’s campaign will no longer air a controversial ad that features Democrat Amy Acton’s estranged mother saying her daughter is a “liar” and “needs help.”

After more than a week of rebukes from both Republicans and Democrats over the content of the ad, Ramaswamy told The Columbus Dispatch that the broadcast spot “ran to completion” as of Oct. 29.

As of Thursday, Ramaswamy’s campaign had spent about $1 million to air the advertisement, though it was originally slated to run through Election Day as part of a $4 million reservation, according to AdImpact data.

Acton has accused her now-deceased stepfather, Cledith Arthur, of sexually abusing her as a child. Donna Arthur, who subsequently lost custody of Acton and stayed with her late husband for years, accuses Acton of lying about her past in the ad.

“Don’t vote for people who lie,” Arthur says. “Don’t let her become your governor.”

The spot conjured a wave of condemnation from Ohio politicians hailing from Ramaswamy’s own party: Outgoing Gov. Mike DeWine urged Ramaswamy to take it down, calling it "despicable” and "deeply, deeply troubling," and Sen. Jon Husted also distanced himself from the commercial.

But President Donald Trump came to the Republican hopeful’s defense last week, asking in a Truth Social post: “Who wouldn't use such an ad? I would, it's called, ‘hitting pay dirt.’” Vice President JD Vance similarly told his party members to “stop whining” about the spot.

Addie Bullock, a spokesperson for Acton’s campaign, called Ramaswamy an “out-of-touch, self-serving billionaire” who will harm anyone to “get what he wants.”

“Vivek Ramaswamy should never have run his despicable ad in the first place, and it’s totally unsurprising that he took it off the air in the most cowardly way possible, without even the hint of an apology to Dr. Acton, her family, or to the people of Ohio,” Bullock said in a statement Thursday.

entries.title: Judge Wants More Details on Trump Administration's Noncitizen Voting Pressure Campaign
entries.summary: The judge noted that the administration can “moot this process at any time” by filing a notice indicating that it will not engage in the election-related conduct Democrats are challenging.
entries.content:
By Michael Kunzelman

A federal judge on Thursday ordered the Trump administration to identify all states where it has pressured officials to comply with its efforts to prevent non-U.S. citizens from voting in the midterm election, inquiries that Democrats have challenged as an illegal power grab.

Chief Judge James Boasberg said he intends to rule by Monday — the eve of Election Day — on a request by Democratic Party leaders to block President Donald Trump's administration from attempting to undermine state election procedures next week.

But the judge noted that the administration can “moot this process at any time” by filing a notice indicating that it will not engage in the election-related conduct the Democratic plaintiffs sued to challenge.

Meanwhile, the judge and plaintiffs want to know if election officials in any states besides California and Washington have received letters from the Justice Department threatening them with criminal prosecution if they knowingly retain noncitizens on their statewide voter registration lists.

Democratic Party leaders, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, sued on Oct. 20 in U.S. district court to prevent Trump from interfering with states’ administration of the election. The plaintiffs asked Boasberg for an order that would bar the Republican president's administration from removing legally registered voters from statewide voter registration lists or preventing states from issuing ballots to registered voters or counting ballots.

The lawsuit cites the administration’s recent actions in California, where the Justice Department sued to block state election officials from counting mail ballots cast by people whom the federal government has identified as “likely” noncitizens until their immigration status can be confirmed. A federal judge on Wednesday sided with California in the case, a ruling the Justice Department immediately appealed.

Administration attorneys claim the government has found evidence that people who aren’t U.S. citizens have or will illegally cast midterm votes. Evidence from the states and the Justice Department's own investigations has shown that voting by noncitizens is extremely rare.

The administration says the plaintiffs’ claims are overly broad, vague and would prevent it from carrying out its constitutional duty to enforce federal laws.

During the hearing, Boasberg expressed doubt that the Democratic plaintiffs have established they have the legal standing necessary to bring their lawsuit's claims. The judge also noted that the administration's letters don't require states to do anything unless the federal government obtains a court order to compel their compliance.

“That's up to them. That's their own choice,” Justice Department attorney Christian Dibblee said. “It just notifies them of a potential violation of federal law.”

Boasberg ordered the administration to turn over its list of Justice Department letter recipients by Friday.

Plaintiffs' lawyer Uzoma Nkwonta urged the judge to stop the government's “unprecedented campaign” to interfere with states' duties to administer elections.

“I don't doubt you have legitimate concerns,” the judge said. “The harder question for me is your standing to do it.”

Boasberg, who was nominated by Democratic President Barack Obama, has been vilified by the White House for rulings against the Trump administration. Trump and his allies called for Boasberg’s impeachment last year after the judge blocked him from using the 18th-century Alien Enemies Act to deport planeloads of Venezuelan migrants to El Salvador.

The lawsuit’s other plaintiffs are the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee and the Democratic Governors Association. Its named defendants are Trump, the Justice Department, Attorney General Todd Blanche, the Department of Homeland Security and its secretary, Markwayne Mullin.
entries.author: The Associated Press

entries.title: Another Dead Person Appears to Have Donated to David Flippo’s House Campaign
entries.summary: The treasurer for the Nevada Republican told The Sun he is “looking into it.”
entries.content:
Another dead person appears to have donated to Republican David Flippo’s campaign for Nevada’s 2nd Congressional District.

In its latest financial disclosure with the Federal Election Commission, the Flippo campaign credited Nevada resident Val Sheldon with contributing $143.56 on Oct. 13.

One problem: The only woman matching Val Sheldon’s information on the filing died in 2019, according to published obituaries from the time reviewed by The Washington Sun. Federal election law generally prohibits political contributions from the deceased, unless someone, prior to their death, arranges “testamentary bequests” to political candidates through their estate.

That doesn’t appear to be the case with Val Sheldon. The Flippo campaign reattributed the $143.56 donation to her after splitting it from a $3,643.56 contribution credited to another Nevada resident named Bret Sheldon — but Bret Sheldon said he knew nothing of this reattribution until The Sun contacted him on Tuesday.

Bret Sheldon’s sister-in-law was Val Sheldon, and he told The Sun he does not know anyone else with that name. He added that the Flippo campaign had not contacted him or received his written consent before reattributing his contribution, which is required under FEC guidelines.

Asked whether the Flippo campaign attributed the donation to someone who’s dead, Thomas Datwyler, Flippo’s campaign treasurer, told The Sun he was “looking into it.”

"Of course, the liberal media is at it again: a $130 contribution under question, in a campaign with over 5,500 individual contributions and $2 million raised for this campaign,” Datwyler added in a statement to The Sun.

While a three-figure political contribution isn’t much money in a race that’s already cost millions of dollars, it may represent a pattern for Flippo. The Wall Street Journal reported earlier this month that the Flippo campaign accepted a $7,000 contribution from Marilynn Mack, which is double the federal limit per election, and reattributed the excess $3,500 to the donor’s mother, Joyce Mack — a well-known Nevada philanthropist who died in 2024.

Rory McShane, a Flippo spokesperson, blamed a clerical error.

Bret Sheldon made a $3,500 donation to Flippo’s campaign after Flippo himself contacted him a few weeks ago. While making his donation, Sheldon opted to cover the payment processing fee, which amounted to $143.56, for his contribution through WinRed — a political fundraising platform used by the Republican Party. WinRed did not respond to a request for comment.

Flippo’s campaign did not answer questions or provide documentation that it had received written confirmation from Bret Sheldon or the individual named Val Sheldon before making the reattribution. The campaign also did not share how it initially identified Val Sheldon.

The dead-donor contributions are the latest troubles for Flippo, who has faced a slew of controversies during his campaign, including campaign finance violations, accusations of exaggerating his military record and questionable circumstances surrounding multiple firings in previous jobs.

Flippo is now in the midst of an unexpectedly tight race against Democrat Theresa Benitez-Thompson in Nevada’s 2nd Congressional District, which President Donald Trump won by double digits in 2020 and 2024.

Benitez-Thompson has attempted to capitalize on Flippo’s controversies, including by running an ad cataloguing Flippo’s troubles.

“Northern Nevadans deserve better than an out-of-town conman who inflates his military record, helps run an apparent Ponzi-like scheme, and hides his personal finances while self-funding his campaign and lying about his donors,” Benitez-Thompson said in a statement to The Sun. “I’m running for Congress because I want to serve our community, not myself or special interests."
Benitez-Thompson (5982x3988, AR: 1.50)Flippo has called Benitez-Thompson “too radical for Nevada” and posted a clip to X of Trump — who endorsed Flippo ahead of the competitive Republican primary — calling her “crazy” during a recent telerally.

Nevada’s 2nd Congressional District has been held by Republicans for over 40 years. A Republican loss here would further damage the party’s already waning chances of preserving a House majority.

But retiring Rep. Mark Amodei, a Republican who’s represented the area for more than a decade, told The Sun he believes Flippo is an “absolutely flawed candidate.”

“You just sit here looking at this stuff, it's like it all looks like bullshit to me,” Amodei told The Sun. “I'm going to say this ain't my guy.”

Amodei has been open about voting for independent candidate Lynn Chapman in the general election.
Mark Amodei AP-25100603916362 (6230x4153, AR: 1.50)Flippo has reported loaning his campaign more than $1.8 million to date. His campaign has faced a slew of campaign finance scrutiny over the last few months, prompting three formal complaints against the candidate. The Nevada Republican also missed the May 15 filing deadline for his required financial disclosure and never filed one for his 2024 congressional campaign.

Flippo eventually completed the document by hand, citing technical difficulties, and provided a copy to The Nevada Independent last month. The financial disclosure still does not appear on the website for the U.S. House Clerk’s Office, which has 30 days to publicly post any reports it has received, as of Thursday.

Mother Jones published several reports cataloguing some mysterious donations to Flippo’s campaign and his connection to one donor with a series of alleged fraud and bad-business dealings levied against him.

Flippo has also faced a string of personal controversies stemming from his career in the financial services industry and his military record. The Washington Post reported last month that Flippo may have been inflating certain details about his military achievements, but the campaign attributed any discrepancies to “honest mistakes” by staff members.

The circumstances surrounding Flippo’s firings as an aircraft maintenance squad commander in 2008 and as a financial adviser in 2024 have also been called into question, but the Nevada Republican’s campaign has largely dismissed the reports as politically motivated attacks and asserted that his “financial licenses are in good standing and active.”

Amodei told The Sun that the information in these reports raises questions about the vetting process Flippo went through before earning the Republican nomination.

“This is all about these guys trying to win, and I get that,” Amodei said, referencing Flippo’s campaign staff. “But the ends justifies the means on steroids is what this feels like.”
entries.author: Jenna Monnin

entries.title: Justice Department Subpoenas California Officials in Escalation of Its Scrutiny of Local Elections
entries.summary: The Los Angeles County registrar said, “threats and intimidated have no place in elections.”
entries.content:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — The U.S. Justice Department on Thursday issued subpoenas to California officials in an escalation of its scrutiny of local election administration.

The subpoenas were being issued by all four U.S. attorneys in California, according to a person familiar with the matter who insisted on anonymity to discuss an ongoing investigation.

Dean Logan, the Los Angeles County registrar, said, “threats and intimidated have no place in elections.”

The Associated Press obtained copies of two subpoenas sent to employees of the Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder to appear in court on Nov. 4, the day after the election.

This follows a federal judge’s appointment of a special master earlier Thursday to evaluate claims by the Trump administration that California has about 20,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls, less than 24 hours after he rejected the Justice Department’s demand that California sequester the ballots until citizenship can be verified.

U.S. District Judge David O. Carter did not specify the exact scope of special master Daniel B. Garrie's responsibilities, but said he would be tasked with “developing the factual record” for the court.

In a Tuesday court hearing, Carter had said he wanted to vet the federal government’s list of over 20,000 alleged noncitizen voters since there has been extensive debate over its reliability and both sides have agreed that it includes an unspecified number of citizens.

Carter also said at the hearing that a special master could investigate California’s claims that it cannot logistically separate the ballots in time for the county election certification deadline on Dec. 3. The federal government has contested that assertion.

It is not clear what would happen if a special master did find a substantial number of noncitizen voters on the federal government’s list or whether it would affect the certification of California’s election results. The 20,000 people on the DOJ’s list constitute only a small fraction of California’s 23 million voters.

Special master appointed amidst Trump administration appeal to higher court

Meanwhile, the Trump administration asked a federal appeals court to quickly weigh in on whether it can temporarily prevent California from counting the disputed ballots. It wants the state to set them aside and only count them if a voter’s citizenship can be verified.

The Justice Department said in a late Wednesday filing that it's essential the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals issue a ruling as soon as possible due to “irreversible ballot processing occurring on an ongoing basis.”

The appeal came just hours after Carter issued a blistering order against the department's last-minute effort to compel California to segregate the ballots from its vote count.

The department says it believes those ballots were sent to people who are registered to vote even though they are not U.S. citizens. Early voting has been underway in the state for weeks and millions of people have already cast ballots.

Trump blasts judge's decision and says California's elections are ‘extremely corrupt’

Carter’s decision was the latest legal setback for President Donald Trump in his efforts to expand federal control over state-run elections in the midterms that will decide control of Congress for the rest of his term. The Justice Department has made similar demands in other states including Washington. Noncitizen voting has been a central focus of Trump’s political messaging for years, although available data indicates it is exceedingly rare.

Trump blasted Carter's ruling against the federal government on Thursday morning before heading to a campaign rally in South Carolina.

“California is very corrupt. The elections are extremely corrupt. The judge should not have done that but we’ll appeal that, of course," he told reporters. Trump added without evidence that there are “hundreds of thousands” and then amended it to “millions, in my opinion” of “bad ballots” in California.

Carter, an appointee of Democratic President Bill Clinton, argued that the Justice Department's demands were a clear violation of the National Voter Registration Act, which prohibits changes to voter rolls or election procedure within 90 days of an election.

A number of US citizens were included in the Justice Department's list of names

Carter also questioned the reliability of the department's list of names, since both sides agree that an unspecified number of citizens were inadvertently included. He argued that separating the ballots at this point would risk disenfranchising citizens and “wreak havoc” on the election certification process.

Over 500,000 votes have already been processed in Los Angeles County alone, according to court filings. The system also protects voter privacy: Once a vote is processed, it cannot be traced back to the person who cast it.

Carter is to rule on the government’s renewed request for a preliminary injunction, which would bar the state from counting the ballots until the litigation is resolved. He said he will do so after a Nov. 13 evidentiary hearing with input from the special master.

He said that if the federal government suspected noncitizens were voting, it could continue to prosecute those cases criminally. Federal authorities have charged over two dozen foreign nationals in California as part of a statewide sweep targeting people officials allege have illegally registered or voted in U.S. elections.

Appeals panel judges have said they wouldn't support setting aside ballots this close to midterms

The Justice Department has argued that it is in the government's interest to prevent fraudulent voting before it happens. Federal prosecutors also have said voters won't be disenfranchised by delaying the tabulation of their ballots while their citizenship is checked — an assertion disputed by county election officials.

The appeal will be the second time that the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals will consider the case.

The first time was just last week when the Justice Department argued before an appeals court panel that a fast ruling on its request was needed to stop any counting of the ballots.

Although the panel ruled it was premature for an appeals court to get involved before a lower-court ruling, two of the three judges wrote separate concurrences making it clear they wouldn’t support setting aside ballots at this late date. They questioned the accuracy of the federal government’s list of alleged noncitizen voters and argued that to set aside votes risks disenfranchising citizens.

One judge dissented, arguing that federal law bars noncitizens from voting and compels California to vet the potentially illegal ballots before they are counted. The failure to do so, he wrote, would cause irreparable harm to the election.

It's not clear whether the case will appear before a new panel of judges or the same three that reviewed the case last time.
